items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Next week the House is in a 1-
week adjournment. When the House resumes on Tuesday, 28 February the Government
will look to conclude the Address in Reply debate. The Government will also progress a
number of readings, particularly first r eadings, on the Order Paper, including further
progress on the Search and Surveillance Bill.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Just seeking an assurance
from the Leader of the House that no se lect committees will be sitting during the
National Party maiden speeches this afternoon.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Not to my knowledge. If there
is something happening that I am not aware of, the member might want to talk to me
off-line about that.
Question No. 1 to Minister

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I seek leave to have this
question moved down to below question No. 12 so that the Prime Minister will have a
chance to answer it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to have question No. 1 relocated to below question
No. 12. Is there any objection to that course of action? There is objection.
Overseas Investment Rules—Judicial Decision on Sale of Crafar Farms
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Has
he had time to read and digest the judgement of Justice Miller regarding the Crafar farm
deal; if so, does he stand by his comments made in the House yesterday?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House)  on behalf of the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: He has read the judgment and he stands by his comments.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: To which law was the Prime Minister referring when he
claimed in the House yesterday that the law—and to use his words—“does not allow
Ministers to reverse OIO advice”?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think what the Prime Minister was referring to was
the requirement that all Ministers act within the law, and that the expectation that the
advice coming from the Overseas Investment Office would, in fact, be within the law.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: That was worse than yesterday.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister yesterday argue that the
Ministers Jonathan Coleman and Maurice W illiamson should rely on the same view as
the Overseas Investment Office?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The expectation of all Minist ers is that they should be
able to rely on the advice of their officials. In relying on that advice, they come to their
own conclusion, within the law.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Do the two Ministers not have their own officials? That
being the case, what scrutiny independent of the Overseas Investment Office—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Stupid question.
482 Questions for Oral Answer 16 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I will say it again very  slowly for the so-called
learned gentleman down there—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: But you heard what he said.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet, and that  will be the end of any further
interjection. I get to my feet to stop this childish backwards and forwards across the
House. I say to the honourable  gentleman on my right that such interjec tions do not
exactly help with good order in the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What scrutiny independent of the Overseas Investment
Office did his Ministers apply to the Overs eas Investment Office report on the Crafar
purchase?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Prime Minister would expect all Ministers to
exercise their judgment based on the advice that is put in front of them. It is patently
obvious that all those decisions are reviewable. That is why we are in this situation now.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We are not going to
get anywhere if we are going to get that sort of answ er. I asked whether the two
Ministers concerned had got  independent advice, inde pendent of the Overseas
Investment Office. That is what I want to know.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In the circumstances I will allow the Rt Hon Winston Peters to
repeat the question he asked, to make sure everyone understands exactly what it is.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What scrutiny independent of the Overseas Investment
Office did his Ministers apply to the Overs eas Investment Office report on the Crafar
purchase?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I doubt that is the first question word for word.
However, what I would say again is that th e Prime Minister expects all Ministers to
exercise their judgment based on the information that is provided to them by their
officials. Their officials, in many cases, are not aligned to the Overseas Investment
Office.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I got the Prime
Minister’s answer, but the question asked of him was did they receive, or did they seek,
any advice independent of the Overseas Investment Office. That is pretty simple.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is correct; his ques tion did exactly ask that. In his
answer the Minister referre d to advice from the offi cials. Although he did not
specifically say the Ministers received advi ce from their own, independent officials, I
picked up that from his answer. But if I am wrong there, he had better correct me. It
seems that that is what the Minister intended.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Did the legal test always re quire the benefits from overseas
ownership to be substantial and identifiable?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: What I understand is  that is the case, but it is the way
in which that conclusion was reached th at is the contention, and, ultimately, the
judgment that has come down. So instead of th at test—better before or after—it is now
with or without. It is a fine technical poi nt. The judge makes that clear. He has also
invited Ministers to reconsider it on that basis, which they will do.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister  ignore section 17 of the
Overseas Investment Act in response to a question in the House yesterday asking how
he had arrived at the view that his two Minist ers, to use his words, had no discretion at
all?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, the first point is the Prime Minister has no
responsibility in this case directly, and he was correct in  saying that his Ministers were
appropriately following advice given to them  by their officials, assessed and judged by
themselves. The point is that the decision, in any event, has been reviewed by the court,
16 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 483
and the court has made a recommendation ab out a reconsideration, and that will take
place.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the reality not that the court did what his Minister failed to
do: it applied the economic benefit test  and found no identifiable evidence that the
overseas buyer would produce any substantial benefit to New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The test applied by the Overseas Investment Office
was the same test that it used to advise a former Minister, the H on David Parker, in his
decisions on these matters. The question is should the test be applied on a before or after
basis, or on a with or without basis? The court has ordered it is with or without, and has
invited Ministers to reconsider, and that is what they will do.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How were the Ministers able to exercise their judgment in this
case, while at the same time following the Prim e Minister’s directi on that they had no
discretion?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think the point is that all of these decisions are
reviewable, and, on the evidence put in front of the Ministers, it was patently clear,
using the before or after test, which has now  been decided is inappropriate, they had—
[Interruption] It was decided that, on the before or  after test, asking the questions that
are required through the four points inside that particular part of the more than 20 points
that have to be considered in the test, they had exercised their judgment appropriately.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to why the public should
not assume that the two Ministers in ques tion took the view that the Prime Minister
keeps on defending, which is that they had no di scretion at all, and therefore applied no
independent thought or judgment at all, and just rubber-stamped the Crafar deal?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Ministers have acted totally appropriately. They
were entitled to believe that the advice they had got from their officials was consistent
with the advice that had been offered over th e previous 7 years. For a large number of
those years the member himself was supporting  the Government in those decisions. It
was never a problem when he was supporting the Government; apparently, it is now.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. He cannot go on to a
personal attack of me when it is well known that he and others got rid of New Zealand
First and Winston Peters because we were stopping their—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The right honour able member knows that  is not a point of
order, under any guise whatsoever. It was successful, though, in stopping the Minister’s
answer. I presume the Minister, therefore, has finished his answer. Yes, he has finished
his answer.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Prime Minister have any other concerns about the way
the Overseas Investment Office is carrying ou t its functions, in light of comments this
morning from the director of the Overseas  Investment Office that in applying the
economic benefit test they never take any account of the economic downside or
economic detriment that might result from foreign investment, such as an increase in the
current account deficit?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No. They have applied the law appropriately for 7
years, and have got to a point where one small aspect of the tests that were put in place
all those 7 years ago does need to be rec onsidered in a different light—so going from
before and after to with or without. I would ask why it is that after, you know, 7 years of
this Act being operative, suddenly those who were party to passing it are so very
concerned—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is sufficient.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Prime Minister now accept that those of us who have
opposed the operation of this system all al ong, such as the Green Party, have been
484 Questions for Oral Answer 16 Feb 2012
absolutely correct to oppose it, because the Overseas Investment Office has been
incorrectly applying the test, as Justice Miller pointed out in the judicial review?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Justice Miller has made that point, and Ministers will
act within that judgment for any future applic ations and for the rec onsideration of this
application. Other than that, the Overseas  Investment Office has operated inside the
bounds that were prescribed in the law by a previous Government.
Overseas Investment Rules—Sale of Crafar Farms
2. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister for Land Information : Does
he believe he and the Government have  conducted themselves competently and
appropriately in relation to the decision to approve the purchase of the Crafar farms by a
foreign buyer; if not, what did they do wrong?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why did the Minister say on se veral occasions th at he had to
approve the sale of the Crafar farms to Shanghai Pengxin under the New Zealand -
China free-trade agreement, when the High Court found that the Overseas Investment
Office’s written advice to him was the opposite?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Because, as I think the Hon Gerry Brownlee told
the House a few minutes ago, for 7 y ears under both a Labour and a National
Government the before and after economic bene fit test was the test that the Overseas
Investment Office used—on the James Came ron application or the Shania Twain
application or any of the others that have gone through it.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Very interesting, but my
question was why he used the cover of the Chinese free-trade agreement—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member may repeat his question.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why did the Minister on several occasions say that he had to
approve the sale of the Crafar farms to Shanghai Pengxin under the New Zealand -
China free-trade agreement, when the High Court found that the Overseas Investment
Office’s written advice to him was the opposite?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Because we were applying the test we believed
to be appropriate—the one that had been used . The fact is that Mi nisters’ decisions are
subject to judicial re view, just like the Hon Chris Cart er lost in the courts over the
Whangamata waterways, and—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. The Minister has still not
addressed the issue—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear what the member’s con cern is. The question specifically
asked why the Minister had said , allegedly on more than on e occasion, that he had to
approve the deal because of the New Zeala nd - China free-trade agreement, which has
nothing to do with the previous practice under  the Overseas Investment Office, because
the New Zealand - China free-trade agreement is relatively recent. That is the bit, I
think, because the question covered only that issue.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I can be helpful.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the Minister can be helpful, I will be very—[Interruption] Order!
If the Minister can be helpful to the House, that is great.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I said in the House in question time on Tuesday
that this application and its  processes went through, regardless of whether we had a
free-trade agreement with China or not.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why did it take 9 months from the time of Shanghai Pengxin’s
application to his erroneous decision? Was it because it took that long for the
Government to stitch up a deal involving Landcorp?
16 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 485

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: It took that long because the Overseas
Investment Office wanted to get all of the relevant information it needed, and it went
back to the applicants on a number of occas ions to further get that information. I am
pleased that the office took the right amount of time, and did not try to rush it.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Can the Minister give an assurance to the House that at no stage
did any Minister of the Government or any official from the Overseas Investment Office
tell any party that they were delaying their decisions until after the election?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Well, that is not what happened, and I most
certainly did not say that; I do not think I can speak for every other human being there
is.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Supplementary question, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What has happened here is that I have just been told by the Hon
Trevor Mallard that the Labour Party is gi ving a further supplementary question to the
Rt Hon Winston Peters. These are meant to be  advised to the Speaker prior to the start
of question time. However—[ Interruption] Order! I do not want to be difficult, but I
just ask members in the future, please, to make  sure that the Speaker is advised of these
things a little more in advance than at the moment that members get to their feet.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I apologise for the late
notice. It will be obvious to everyone that the answers are the reason for—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not an acceptable point  of order either. It was barely
much better than the one we he ard not so long ago. It was ju st being used to criticise
another member of this House, and that is not allowed under the point of order process.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I apologise, Mr Speaker. I will get you notice, next time,
much earlier, but it was the nature of the quest ion. I want to ask the Minister this: if he
is explaining the proper due diligence done by the Overseas Investment Office on the
issues he talks about as taki ng 9 months, why then did it  take over 12 months for the
same office to determine that May Wang and Jack Chen were of good character, when
one phone call to the Shanghai or Hong Kong stock exchange would have told them
otherwise?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I do not know whether I can ever comment on
the process that the Overseas Investment Of fice goes through. It took its time to make a
determination about the bid. And in the case of Natural Dairy—the member will be
pleased—the Overseas Investment Office recommended that the Government not
approve it.
Economy—2012 Budget Policy Statement
3. JONATHAN YOUNG (National—New Plymouth)  to the Minister of Finance:
What reports has the Government issued on the economy?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: The Government has today issued th e Budget Policy Statement for 2012. It
confirms the Government’s clear and comp rehensive economic plan for the next 3
years, which will make our economy more competitive so it can fulfil its potential.
Within this plan the Government has set out four main priorities to help achieve this.
They are to continue to responsibly manage  the Government’s finances by returning to
surplus and keeping debt under control; to continue to implement economic policies that
build a more competitive, export-focused economy; to deliver better public services to
New Zealanders within a tight fiscal Budge t; and to rebuild our second-biggest city,
Christchurch.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: How will the Government’s economic plan be reflected in Budget
486 Questions for Oral Answer 16 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As the Budget Policy Stat ement says, Budget 2012 will be,
first and foremost, about sticking to the G overnment’s economic plan. It is important
that we do that to build a stronger, mo re competitive economy that supports more
sustainable jobs and higher incomes, and ensures that New Zealand starts to pay its way
in the world. Indeed, the Government’s B udget priorities throughout this parliamentary
term will be about sticking to that plan.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: What does the Budget Policy St atement say about the outlook for
the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Budget Policy Statem ent sets out some updated
forecasts from Treasury. They show that  New Zealand’s economic outlook, although
somewhat weaker than forecast in the pre- election update in Oct ober, remains positive.
Our terms of trade are expected to remain high. Our largest trading partners, particularly
China and Australia, are among the stronger-performing countries in the world. And the
rebuilding of Christchurch will provide impetus to the economy in coming years.
However, there is a risk that events offs hore, particularly in Europe, could have a
negative impact on the New Zealand economy. The Government continues to monitor
those events closely.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does the Budget Policy Statement show a rising current account
deficit, as well as higher Government debt and lower growth in the coming years than
were promised by National during the election?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Budget Policy Statem ent does show a worsening
economic situation, which has a negative impact  on the balance of payments and one or
two of the other matters the member raises. A nd that has effectively caused, as stated in
the Budget Policy Statement, a delay to the Canterbury rebuild, brought about by the
additional seismic activity and also the more troubling clouds in Europe in the
economies over there. So those things all ha ve an impact on the predictions in this
particular statement.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: And how is the latest economic outlook expected to impact on the
Government’s finances?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Budget Policy Statement forecasts show that the
Government remains on track to post a $370 million surplus in 2014-15, to keep net
debt below 30 percent of GDP, and to re duce this to 20 percent of GDP by 2020-21.
Given the events in Europe and the weakened  outlook for global growth, this forecast is
understandably smaller than was forecast in the pre-election update, but the Government
does remain on its fiscal track to surplus. It  will, however, require disciplined control of
spending and tight management of our capit al allocations. For example, we have
conferred net zero capital allowances for each  of the next five Budgets, requiring new
investments to be funded from capital freed up  from the balance sheet rather than by
additional borrowing.
Benefits—Work and Income Case Management Approach
4. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does
she have confidence that Work and In come meets their own “case management
approach” expectations?
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Associate Mi nister of Social Development)  on
behalf of the Minister for Social Development: Yes. Work and Income deals with 147
million transactions a year. That is 2.8  million transactions a week and 403,000
transactions a day. The Minist er believes Work and Income staff work very hard and
she backs them.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she believe the level of support a sole parent on the domestic
purposes benefit can access in order to move into work or education is sufficient?
16 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 487

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Yes; there are a number of  benefits and assistance
packages that women on the domestic pur poses benefit, or anyone on the domestic
purposes benefit, can access in order to get into education. It depends on which level of
education they wish to access as to how thos e benefits will be applied. But they are
available, for instance, for university study in  the form of student loans and allowances;
for lower-level qualifications—levels 1, 2, a nd 3—that they are seeking, they can still
receive the training incentive allowance.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: How much can someone on the domestic purposes benefit who
wants to move into education, and who has one dependent child and no income, receive
per hour per child to assist with childcare?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: It is a very precise question, given the primary
question, but as I understand it a person on the domestic purposes benefit with one child
is able to receive the normal domestic pur poses benefit. She may well be entitled to
accommodation supplements on top of that. Sh e is also entitled to early childhood
education and childcare allowances on top of that. She is able to receive student loans in
respect of meeting the fees for each paper,  and also a $1,000 grant for course-related
costs.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I seek leave to table the details of the childcare subsidy, which
states that the mother shall be—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Before we go into that, what is the source of this document?

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: It is available publicly, but given the Minister was unable to
answer the specific question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That was just grandstanding; we do not do that under a point
of order. Silly me! Let me reword that. We should not do that under a point of order.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: What is the difference in support a solo mum with one dependent
child and no income will be eligible for if she wishes to study and approaches
StudyLink versus if that same solo mother went to Work and Income, and why is there
such a difference?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I call the Hon Chester Borrows, in so far as he is able to give an
answer, in the breadth of the primary question.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I would draw attention to the breadth of this question
away from the primary question, which relate d to expectations of people approaching a
case manager at Work and Income.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The original question
obviously relates to an issue of the day, wher e Work and Income have given inadequate
advice to a domestic purposes benefit mum, and part of that was her getting very
different advice from both StudyLink and Work and Income. So all of this does relate to
the adequacy of the advice that Work and Income staff—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! My advice to the member is, if she wants Ministers to have
that kind of detail available to answer que stions, make the primary question more clear.
With all respect, this primary question is very  broad and it is not reasonable to expect
that the Minister could have that level of detail, given that primary question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: To what does she attribute our status as having one of the highest
rates of unemployment for sole parents in th e OECD, next to Turkey and Malta: a lack
of willingness to work, as her welfare reform package implie s, or the barriers to work,
as the reality suggests?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: The finding on New Zealand’ s provision of services
to people wishing to study who are in receipt  of a domestic purposes benefit, in respect
of other OECD countries, was not made by th e Minister but in f act by an independent
organisation. It is interesting to note that th ere is lots of assistance available to sole
parents. Even without the training incenti ve allowance, there is extensive support
488 Questions for Oral Answer 16 Feb 2012
available for domestic purposes benefit recipi ents studying at tertiary level, including
interest-free student loans, student allowa nces, childcare subsidies, the accommodation
supplement, out-of-school care and recreati on subsidies, 20 hours’  free early childhood
education, temporary additional support, speci al-needs grants, and so on, and these are
not available in many other countries.
Benefits—Effect of Training Incentive Allowance Changes
5. JAN LOGIE (Green)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does she have
concerns that changes to the eligibility for the Training Incentive Allowance are causing
single parent beneficiaries to consider working in the sex industry?
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Associate Mi nister of Social Development)  on
behalf of the Minister for Social Development: No.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Does she think it is fa ir that single-parent beneficiary Tania Wysocki is
reluctantly considering sex work to cover th e cost of travel and childcare associated
with her high-level veterinary nursing degr ee, whereas these costs would be covered by
the training incentive allowance were she studying for a lower-level course?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I find it very difficult to  accept that somebody is
forced into prostitution in order to st udy. People may have to choose between earning
an income through work, and studying. There ar e no easy options for a solo parent, but
there is considerable support available, as outlined in answer to the previous question.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Does she accept that the childcare subsidy offered to Tania Wysocki does
not cover the full costs of childcare, wher eas the training incentive allowance would
meet the additional costs beyond the subsidy?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Ms Wysocki was quoted in an article from the New
Zealand Herald, and the subsidies available to Ms Wysocki are not those quoted in the
New Zealand Herald. The reporter was given an indica tion of those subsidies orally; he
chose not to write them. It is important to note that Ms Wysocki receives the equivalent
of a salary of $43,000 a year plus her entitlement to 20 hours’ early childhood
education. I think most New Zealanders would find that an equivalent salary of $43,000
is sufficient, or at least reasonable.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Does it concern her that it took a visit with Tania’s local MP, Paul
Hutchison; a letter to  John Key; unanswered corresponde nce with the Mi nister’s own
office; multiple conversations with Work a nd Income; and, finally, media attention for
Tania to receive her full benefit entitlements, a nd that even then this offer of assistance
is not enough to keep her from considering se x work as a way to make ends meet while
studying?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I refer to my answer to the previous supplementary

District Health Boards—Results of Collaboration
6. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Minister of Health : What improvements
have there been to services for patients as a result of greater collaboration between
District Health Boards?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Hutt Valley District Health Board
and the Capital and Coast District Health Bo ard have been working together to provide
faster access to magnetic resonance imaging fo r their patients. In March last year, I am
told, there were 760 patients waiting longer than 6 months to have routine magnetic
resonance imaging at Wellington Regional Ho spital. That waiting list has now been
completely cleared and no one is waiting longer than 4 months. More scans are now
being done at the Hutt Hospital and an after-hours radiology registrar has been provided
there instead of relying on services from Australia. This is a very good example of what
can be achieved when neighbouring district health boards work together.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What improvement has there been to waiting times for ultrasounds
in Wairarapa?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Hutt Valley District H ealth Board and the Wairarapa
District Health Board have worked together  to reduce the waiting time for ultrasounds
from 9 months last year to less than 2 m onths today. Additional clinics provided at Hutt
490 Questions for Oral Answer 16 Feb 2012
Hospital have cleared the backlog, and now a sonographer is travelli ng from the Hutt
Valley to Masterton for a clinic 1 day per w eek. This more efficient service sees fewer
cancellations, less rebooking, and more certa inty for patients, and is a very good
example of district health boards working together to provide faster services for
patients.

expecting, and has been working within, a ra nge of $5 billion to $7 billion resulting
from the asset sales.

items.text: Why has the Government only now woken up to the fact,
via Mr English’s comments in the media in th e last 24 hours, that there is a high risk of
its 51 percent controlling interest being diluted, when a Treasury report entitled
Extending the Mixed Ownership Model , dated 4 March 2011, warned that if the
Government wants to keep its majority st ake then “any further raisings will require

Minister’s comments that the reason for the asset sale float was because the

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL

Local Authorities—Rates Increases Since 2002
8. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National—Botany)  to the Minister of Local Government :
What analysis has he received on rate increases across New Zealand’s 78 councils
following the enactment of new local government legislation in 2002?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The analysis shows that
the national rates bill has increased quite dr amatically, from $2.3 billion a year to $4.2
billion a year, or by 7 percent compound per an num. Inflation over these years has been
3 percent per annum. The increases range fr om as high as 13 percent compounded per
year for some councils, to the lowest of 4 percent compounded per year for others. None
of the councils were able to k eep the increase over that decade  to the rate of inflation.
The fact that these rate rises dramatical ly increased under the enactment of the new
local government legislation in  2002 raises questions abou t the negative impacts these
reforms have had for both households and businesses.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Has the Minister seen any reports from 2002 where the Government
assured businesses, farmers, and householde rs that the changes to the purposes and
principles of local government would have no impact on rates or co sts, and given what
has transpired since, what economic impacts have these changes had?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, I have seen reports. St rong assurances were given by
the previous Government, in fact, that there would be bi g cost savings from those
changes in 2002. The fact is that the average rate rise in the decade since has been 6.8
percent, as compared with the decade previous of 3.9 perc ent per annum. If the rate
increase had continued at the previous ra te, rates would be costing the New Zealand
economy today $1 billion a year less, or a saving of $500 per household. As a
consequence of these figures, the Government is reviewing those 2002 changes, because
ongoing cost increases of this order are not affordable and will negatively impact on
New Zealand’s economic prospects.
Earthquakes, Canterbury and Christchurch—Extension of Red Zone Offer to
Retirement Villages
9. Hon LIANNE DALZIEL (Labour—Christchurch East)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
items.text: Does he stand by the part of his statement of 27
January, announcing the extension of the red z one offer to retirement villages, that
letters of offer would be sent to each re sident and CERA would work with village
owners as quickly as possible to ensure the residents are assisted; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It
was always the Government’s intention that  red zone offers would go to residents.
Receivables from the sale of retirement villa ges to the Crown must be applied to exit
payments to residents via a statutory superv isor as a priority over any other person,
including the owners, so that the residents’ interests are protected.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Why was the wording of the media statement, which said a
letter of offer would be sent to each re sident, changed to the one now on the Beehive
website, which says that an offer to each ow ner will follow, and was that designed to
cover up the humungous blunder, as one pers on has described th is communication of
this policy?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, it is because the legalities around this mean that
the owners of the re st home own the property—have the title to the property. The
residents, in the cases we are generally talking about, have a licence to occupy. So by
law—by one law—the settlement is with the owners, but, as I said before, receivables
from the sale of retirement villages to the Crown must be applied to exit payments to
residents as a priority over any other person, including the owners, so that the residents’
interests are protected.

Events, Major—Legislative Protection
12. Hon TAU HENARE (National)  to the Minister for Economic Development :
What progress has he made declaring th e Volvo Ocean Race Stopover a major event
under the Major Events Management Act 2007?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Very good
progress has been made. A paper has been  approved by a Cabine t committee, and I
expect the Government next week to endorse  the declaration of the Volvo Ocean Race
stopover next month in Auckland. Major ev ents such as these are a significant
contributor to New Zealand’s economy, so there are a number of protections in the
Major Events Management Act. For example—and I pick a random example—as the
author of the Act said at the time it was passed, “The bill … prohi bits the on-sale of
tickets at above their face value. As recen t events show, those who buy up tickets and
then seek to sell them at an unfair profit have depriv ed many Kiwi … fans of the
opportunity to attend big events.”

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Why are these kinds of prot ections under the Major Events
Management Act necessary?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Event organisers need to be confident that their investment
and marketing are not undermine d. As the author of the Act said at the time, organisers
and sponsors make huge financial commitments to make these types of events a reality,
and clearly they do not want others to free -ride on their investments and trade off their
goodwill. Indeed, there are those who would a dvocate these protections be extended to
regional events, such as—I do not know; speaking hypothetically—Wellington’s
Homegrown festival, although presumably not, in this case, the origin al sponsor of this
Act.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What reports has the Minister  received that suggest ongoing
behaviour contrary to the intent of that legislation?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have received a report as late as this morning highlighting
the problem of ongoing ticket scalping for upc oming events, taking place in this case,
apparently, from a red-painted ticket sales o ffice in Naenae, which is possibly part of a
chain of such offices all across Lower Hutt. Notwithstanding that the alleged perpetrator
has been quoted in the paper as saying “It’s not what it looks like.”, I think in this case it
is what it looks like, and what it looks like is a clear case of “Do as I say, but not as I
do.”

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Dr Russel Norman and from the Rt Hon

The urgent debate procedure is a means of holding the Government to account for

occur in the future. There is no ministerial responsibility for the decision of the High

for the decision of the High Court requi ring that the Ministers’ decision be

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to speak
in this Address in Reply debate, because of the excellent record of the National
Government over the last 3 years, and becau se of the extremely well-crafted 120-point
economic development plan, which heralds such  a bright future for all New Zealanders.
But I must say I was somewhat concerned last Tuesday when I heard some somewhat
vacuous huffing and puffing from the deput y leader of the Labour Party, Grant
Robertson, the member for Wellington Central,  when he said after a 10-minute tirade
that, in his view, all the National Government  could do was sell, cu t, and hope. That is
why Mr Robertson has only 33 colleagues sittin g on those benches over there, and if he
continues with the lack of in sight he displayed last week , there will be some fewer
members left next time around.
What was extraordinary about Mr Robertson’s lack of insi ght was that he failed to
recognise that election 2011 was all about a National Government that was committed
and determined to balance the books by 2014, committed and determined to achieve
economic growth through a sustainable 120- point plan, and committed and determined
to follow prudential financial management, versus a Labour Opposition, which seemed
hell-bent, committed, and determined to spend more, borrow more, get money from
wherever it could, and tax more at a time when this was clearly against the short-,
medium-, and long-term interests of New Zealand.
The other thing that was notable about the Opposition was that it accused both the
Prime Minister and members from this side of failing to address the social issues. It is as
though the Labour Opposition has this myopic feeling that it possesses the high ground
on social justice and other su ch things. How wrong could it be! We have just seen a
landmark initiative from the Hon Paula Bennett in initiating the extremely important
Green Paper for Vulnerable Children. It  is of extreme importance to all New
Zealanders.
Everyone in this House knows that child outcomes have deteriorated in New Zealand
relative to OECD statistics over the last 30 years since the 1960s, and everybody in this
House knows that probably in the order of 15  to 20 percent of our children will not
achieve their full potential or will not re alise their dreams unless a huge amount of
effort is put into solving what has gone on for decades. It is a particularly difficult
situation, and it will not be solved easily. However, the Hon Paula Bennett is holding
meetings throughout the country that are ex tremely well attended, and she is giving
ordinary Kiwis the opportunity to turn up and show what th ey believe is important in
solving these fundamentally serious situations for New Zealand.
I would say to all members of  this House that they shoul d take note of that. They
should read the green paper, and, hopefully, they too can contribu te by a submission to
the green paper. It is extremely politically neutral in the way it has been written, and it
does indeed give a great opportunity—
Su’a William Sio: I want you to be the Minister.
500 Address in Reply 16 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: —for a contribution, and I am sure Su’a William Sio over
there will be doing exactly that. He attended the meeting in M āngere, and I very much
hope he will be a major contributor.
There is indeed a groundswell throughout New Zealand that improving outcomes for
children is a major, major issue in New Zeal and and does require a far greater priority
than successive Governments have put to it over the last few decades. That is why the
National Government has demonstrated its  willingness to improve child outcomes by
forming a high-level ministerial gr oup on poverty, by agreeing to hold a M āori Affairs
Committee inquiry into the dete rminants of well-being for M āori children, by initiating
the green paper, and—only yesterday—by ini tiating a Health Committee inquiry into
what practical health and social interventi ons can be made to prevent child abuse and
promote child well-being from conception unti l 3 years of age, which is the most vital
time to prevent problems developing.
As a young house surgeon at Middlemore Hospita l, several decades ago, I am afraid
to say—I admit that—it was deeply impresse d on me the predictability of cycles of
disadvantages that were going to occur. In the antenatal clinics I would see these young
women and their babies. They were clearly hi ghly at risk. Sadly, often they would be
single, they would have tatt oos, they would be smokers, th ey would be addicted to
drugs, and they would often be in the lower socio-economic group. Again, sadly, a
higher proportion of them would be Māori or Pacific Islanders.
Those children, having been born, woul d often go to suboptimal housing. They
would often go to homes where their ear infe ctions were not treated, where their sores
were not treated, where they did not get thei r immunisations or their Well Child checks.
They went to school, they did not learn well, and they would finally leave school
without appropriate qualificati ons. They could not get a job, they turned to crime, and
they got caught, because they could not even hear the policeman coming.
It is worthwhile pointing out that a st udy by a fellow called Bowers in the 1980s of
the muster at Mt Eden Prison showed that 90 percent of the muster had some sort of
hearing defect and there were 15 to 20 of those prisoners wandering around with
chronically suppurating ears. These are the very things that we have got to solve. All the
literature—the scientific, the psychological, the educative, the j udicial—points to early
intervention. That is why it is so importa nt that the Government’s initiatives on
vulnerable children must be carried through, and, hopefully, the whole Parliament will
get behind it. That is why the M āori Affairs Committee inquiry into improving M āori
children’s outcomes is so important, and that is why the Health Committee inquiry into
practical, evidence-based outcomes that can be taken from the earliest stage is of
extreme importance and gives all members of this House an opportunity to contribute.
Finally, I just wanted to say that clea rly the economic influences to resource
excellent health, education, and social services are not everything; practical focus on the
economy and on economic growth is absolutely vital. It is vital and fundamental that
this National Government is determined to sustained economic growth through this very
well-crafted economic development plan, through prudential financial management, and
through balancing the books by 2014-15. This is particularly important in these very
uncertain economic times, and it is particularly important for us to ensure that there are
practical resources behind making the outcomes for children in New Zealand better than
they are at present.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, I want to congratulate you
and your fellow presiding officers on your re-e lections to office, and also to all
returning members to the House, congratulat ions on your re-electi ons, and to all new
members, congratulations on your elections . To the new members who have already
made their maiden speeches, congratulat ions—particularly to my four Labour
16 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 501
colleagues David Clark, Andrew Little, Dr  Megan Woods, and Rino Tirikatene on the
superb speeches that they made the other ni ght in the House—and also to all the other
members who have made their maiden spee ches. To those who have not yet made
maiden speeches, best of luck. It is a great experience and one to really treasure.
I feel it is a great privilege to be able to speak in the Address in  Reply debate to the
Speech from the Throne, and particularly to support the amendment that has been
moved by my friend and colleague our new l eader, David Shearer. I want to read the
amendment in full because it merits repeating: “and the National-led Government will
sell New Zealand’s assets against the will of  the public; the Government has no ideas to
create jobs or a clean and innovative New Zealand; that the Government is widening the
gap between the very rich and the rest and therefore this House has no confidence in the
National-led government.” That amendment ha s my wholehearted sup port, and that of
my colleagues, and it has been reinforced by the handling of the Crafar farms affair.
It is useful, I think, to just mention a bit of the background to that matter. The
Shanghai Pengxin company made an offer for the Crafar farms. That was accepted by
receivers KordaMentha early last year, but it was conditional on Shanghai Pengxin
getting Overseas Investment Office approval. It should be remembered that those farms
total nearly 8,000 hectares a nd they comprise 16 central and southern North Island
properties. They have been in receivership for more than 2 years.
The receivers gave Shanghai Pengxin unt il 31 January 2011 to make its offer,
understood to be worth between $210 million and $220 million, unconditional. On
Friday, 20 January the Overseas Investme nt Office did provide its recommendation on
the sale to the Minister for Land Information, the Hon Maurice Williamson, and
Associate Minister of Finance, the Hon Jonathan Coleman. After this, Shanghai
Pengxin waited until 27 January 2012 for the Mi nisters involved to re ach a decision to
allow the purchase to proceed.
The success of the bid relied heavily on the involvement of Landcorp, a State-owned
enterprise, in operating the farms, as Sha nghai Pengxin could not pr ove that it had any
relevant experience and skill in farming pract ices. It is underst ood that Landcorp, on
behalf of the taxpayer, had agreed to pa y $18 million a year, effectively to rent the
farms back from Shanghai Pengxin. Landcorp, of course, had earlier bid for the farms
but was unsuccessful.
A Kiwi consortium last year offered $171.5 million for the farms, to be divided
amongst members of the consortium. Receivers said the offer was too cheap, and
KordaMentha reminded everybody concerned that  it was legally obliged to try for the
highest price for the estate. That was the decision that was taken to the Overseas
Investment Office; that was the matter that  was taken on to the High Court judicial
review on 3 February. The decision yesterday by Justice Miller to overturn the Shanghai
Pengxin sale means that the office must rec onsider its recommendation in light of the
interpretation that was set out by the High Court in its decision.
There are three points that I think it is worth having on the record of the House about
the decision. In setting aside the decision, the court said, first, that the Ministers
involved misdirected themselves on the law, and that the essence of the misdirection
was that comparing Shanghai Pengxin’s bid on ly against the status quo of the farms,
rather than against what another New Z ealand investor would do with them—which
was deemed likely to be similar to Sh anghai Pengxin’s development plans—was a
fundamental error.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: The same process Labour had used during its time in
office.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Then Ministers ignored—and we hear from one of the
Ministers in error that this was a proce ss that has been used down the ages. Well,
502 Address in Reply 16 Feb 2012
actually, he knows that is not right, because it is not the process that the Hon David
Parker employed in respect of the Auckland International Airport. He did something
that that Minister refused to do—apply his own judgment in the national interest to the
decision. Instead of just saying “We will flog it to the highest bidder, because that suits
us.”, he asked what was actually in New Z ealand’s national interest, and that is the
difference between the previous admi nistration under Labour and the current
administration. We actually did think about  what mattered for New Zealand and we
made decisions accordingly.
The second key part of the decision of Justi ce Miller was that Ministers were held to
have ignored clear evidence of the benefits that would accrue should the land remain in
New Zealand ownership. Given that economic benefits would also be realised if the
farms were sold to a New Zealand buyer, the Shanghai Pengxin bi d could not claim to
be adding substantial benefit to the country, and that is a basic and fundamental problem
with the reasoning process used by the Ministers.
Finally—and, I think, most damningly—t he Ministers’ error was not a mere
technicality and the economic benefits caused by the overseas investment were
materially overstated. It is going to be very hard, despite what we have heard in answers
to questions to Ministers, when this decisi on has to be taken agai n, for that bid to be
upheld—very, very hard, indeed. The High Cour t’s decision to overt urn the sale shows
that National simply got it wrong, and in doing so, as I said earlier, just ignored the best
interests of New Zealanders.
It is worse than that, because if one l ooks at the entire process, there are some
suspicions that are naturally arising as a result of the way in which the process was
handled. It seems pretty clear, actually, stepping back, that the Government always
intended to sell this valuable land to Sh anghai Pengxin, despite cl ear evidence that it
was not the right decision for New Zealand. John Key has repeatedly claimed that the
law did not allow him or his Ministers to overrule a recommendation made by the
Overseas Investment Office to approve the Chinese consortium’s application. That is
plainly wrong, and that is certainly very different to the sort  of reasoning process
employed, for example, by David Parker. Ju stice Miller’s decisi on shows that John
Key’s claim was wrong and that this was simply a way of justifying erroneous decision-
making on the part of the two Ministers whom I have referred to. Mi nisters do have the
ability—clear ability—to turn down reco mmendations by the Overseas Investment
Office.
The test is very clear in the Act. They are not entitled to depart from the tests in the
Act, but they are entitled and required to appl y their own judgment to that test. In fact,
the Act goes so far as to say that once they  have received the advice from the office,
they can consult with whomever they like in reaching their final decision. There is
simply no evidence that either of these Mi nisters applied the independent judgment in
the interests of the country that we would expect them to.
We on this side of the House said that the decision to sell to Shanghai Pengxin was
wrong. It was not in New Zeal and’s national interest. We all want foreign direct
investment, but we do not want  to sell valuable land to foreign investors only to see
profits that could have been reaped by New Zealand farmers and injected into our own
economy heading offshore.
John Key has repeatedly warned that ther e is a risk that New Zealanders could
become tenants in our own land. Well, this is now his chance to make sure that that does
not happen in this case. We need to be setting a high standard for any further
investment. We need an absolute assurance that any investment will add more value and
provide more opportunities for New Zealande rs, and above all, we need competent
Ministers with a plan to build a prosperous, fair, and vibrant society.

items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, I

I cannot let that last speech go without point ing out one or two things. The thing that
really struck me is that those guys over th ere did one thing in G overnment and are now
saying another thing in Opposition. Of course , there is a word for that, but we do not
need to go into that. But the facts bear this out. Under the first term of this National
Government, 100,000 hectares of land were so ld. Under the 9 years of the Labour

items.text: —of land were sold—666,000 hectares. In 1

Charles Chauvel to get up now and say that he  is opposed to land sales to foreigners is

So I think the public are going to see this for what it is, but what these people over

But there is good news too, because today we  have had the Budget Policy Statement.
Look, the Budget Policy Statement shows that we are on track economically. John Key,
the best Prime Minister that this country ha s ever had, said he would get the economics
of this country on the right track. [ Interruption] The new New Zealand First member
Tracey Martin can go and have a read of this; it is a very good piece of paper—in fact, a
number of pieces of paper. We are on track  to post a surplus of $370 million by 2014-
15—responsible management of the finances th at Labour was never ab le to deliver. It
wasted 9 years squandering every single opportun ity. We could be so far ahead if it had
not raided the cookie jar year after year to buy off votes from every community
imaginable.
There is an essential choice that the vot ers of New Zealand made at the general
election. They voted for the mixed-ownershi p model, because, unl ike these guys, the
New Zealand public understands we have to get debt down. But we have also got to
build infrastructure. We have got $250 billion worth of assets and wh at we are going to
do, in order to buy infrastructure that the count ry needs, is partially float four of those
companies. What I want to know, Maryan Stre et, if this is such a bad idea, while you
guys were in office why did you not buy back the 25 percent of Air New Zealand that—
[Interruption] Yep, see, she is playing the violin. Why did they not do it? The fact is
they had the opportunity. Their opposition to this is purely political, but if they had their
16 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 505
way, they would be borrowing more. We would be getting into more debt. We would be
going down the route of Greece, Ireland, Spain, and Portugal.
We are on track, and we are on track becau se we are making the decisions that are
right for New Zealand. So I am very proud  to be a member of this National-led
Government. The future is excellent for New Zealand if we stick to the economic track
that we are on. If these people ever get back in charge, I can tell you the outlook is not
going to be good at all. But, fortunately, wh at I can assure members and the public is
that these people are so far away from making an impact, it is negligible—years away. I
do not think that the next Labour Prime Minist er, frankly, is even in  the Parliament. In
fact, who is the Leader of the Opposition?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who is he?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I do not know. Is it Winston?

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: It could be.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Well, it could be. It coul d be the leader of the
Green Party, because that is a leaderless rabble.
Paul Hutchison talked about the 120-poi nt economic plan. It is about economic
growth, it is about looking outwards, and it is about getting investment into New
Zealand and growing the economy. That myopi c look that says: “Don’t come here if
you are a Chinese investor, please.”, that is not going to work. We have got to get the
capital into this country, we  have got to raise exports, we  have got to get the country
going. It needs clear-sighted vision, and that  is what the mixed-ownership model is
bringing—a very clear view on what New Zealand needs.
So those are my remarks. We have laid ou t our stall: a clear pl an, a clear delivery.
The public are behind us. It is the way to go.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a great pleasure  to rise and speak in
this Address in Reply debate. Can I start by sa ying that it is going to be a very hard act
to follow that wonderful, delightful, entert aining, visionary speech from the Minister
Jonathan Coleman—

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: You’ll be all right, Todd. Don’t worry. You’ll be all right.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: —but I will do my very best, Maryan Street; you are absolutely
right. But that was an excellent speech. The Minister touched on all of the points that
were important to New Zealanders last year  before the election—all of the reasons why
New Zealanders turned out in  their droves to su pport this party and the Prime Minister
and to say “We want more of that for another 3 years.”
Can I say that it is great to be back, and it  is enjoyable to be back in this House to
join with my colleagues and, particularly, to join with other members of Parliament here
from all parties as we look towards the ne xt 3 years to work hard, collectively and
separately, to make New Zealand a better place. I particularly want to recognise the role
of the Speaker, and the deputies and assistan ts, to congratulate the Speaker on his
election and reappointment, and to say that we look forward to more time with him in
the Chair.
Can I recognise the new members of Pa rliament who have come here, and
particularly members from the Green Party. I thoroughly enjoyed their maiden speeches
yesterday, although not as much, perhaps, as  my colleague on my right, Cam Calder.
But can I say, it is good to see new members coming here and talking a bit about why
they have come to this House and what brought them here, and so on.
I want to recognise members of New Zeala nd First, the new members to the House,
and their contributions in their maiden speech es. They too were enjoyable. I want to
welcome back the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who has come back to the House, and also,
of course, to welcome back the Hon John Banks. They are brothers at times—perhaps in
the past. It is good to see those members back. We may not agree on everything, but it is
506 Address in Reply 16 Feb 2012
good to have members of the House who will come here and debate issues honestly.
May I wish them well in that.
Can I recognise four members of Labour w ho are new to this Parliament and who
gave their maiden speeches yesterday; toda y we have seven new members of National
who will make their speeches—7-4. That would have been a good score some years ago
in a Rugby World Cup when the All Blacks we re playing Australia or somebody else. I
want to reflect on that for a moment. Here we are, a National Government in a second
term, which in the last 3 years went thr ough, with New Zealand, some very difficult
times: the global financial crisis, the steepe st recession New Zealand has faced in 60
years, great heartache to New Zealand and Ne w Zealanders with the devastation of the
earthquakes, and the very sad loss of life in Christchurch. But here we are with seven
new members of the National caucus making their speeches today, and well done to
them.
That is a bit about rejuvenation. Three years ago we saw rejuvenation for New
Zealand when New Zealanders in droves—the largest vote ever cast for any party under
MMP—decided they wanted a change of direc tion and they wanted a brighter future.
And here we are with seven new Nati onal MPs to make their speeches today—
rejuvenation after only one term.
On the Opposition side, in Labour, there are four new members. Actually, there were
some very good speeches there but only four of them. What happened to Labour over
that last 3 years when it decided that it was about li stening to New Zealanders,
rejuvenating, and bringing in new blood? Well, I feel very sorry for some of their hard-
working MPs who 3 years ago made thei r maiden speeches with some of my
colleagues—some very intelligent MPs who are no longer in this place. So there is some
work to do.
Can I say that in mentioning Mr Peters, we should actually have a vote in this House
about who the real Leader of the Oppositio n is, because I think, based upon what has
happened so far over the last 2 weeks, it is not clear that the party in Opposition with the
largest number of votes would necessarily win there. If we think about—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: I’ll go with the Australian. I’m going to vote for the
Australian.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: Mr Williamson would vote for the Australian—very good. Can I
say here that over the last 2 weeks, when  we think about question time and about the
Opposition holding the Government to account we see that the largest party in this
House, Labour, has been woefully neglectful and absent. And can I say that although we
will not always agree with everything that ha ppens from all parties in this House, if
nothing more it has been interesting and ente rtaining to listen to the Rt Hon Winston
Peters. I say to his colleagues that they too ha ve a very important role to play. You see,
the thing about Opposition is that it is not always about opposing everything; it is about
finding ways that we can work together, putting the politics aside from time to time, and
finding ways that we can work together.
New Zealand First members have a list MP  based in the Bay of Plenty—Brendan
Horan—and I had a chance to talk to him for the first time last week and welcome him
to Parliament on behalf of parts of the Bay of Plenty and with my National colleagues in
all the other seats in the Bay of Plenty, wh ich not only did we hold before but we were
able to continue to hold in this election. I talked to him about putting aside some of our
individual political issues and finding ways to  work together more closely so that we
can do better for New Zealanders. And I look fo rward to being able to do that with New
Zealand First members.
Finally, I want to get on to a bit of the de tail of some of the things the Government
has set out to do, but before I do I want to fo cus on one thing, and that is the leader of
16 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 507
the Labour Party, David Shearer. He came into Parliament at the same time as some of
us, a short 3 years ago—3 years and a few mo nths. I really got to know him only when
we played in the Parliamentary cricket ga me in Cambridge a couple of years ago. It
strikes me that that is about the same am ount of knowledge that most New Zealanders
have on him. But do I wish him well? Absolu tely. It seems that he was demoted or
dropped from the Big Gay Out last week. I did not see a lot of coverage there. Breakfast
TV—in the headlines today, Breakfast has decided that as leader of Labour and Leader
of the Opposition, he is not that  interesting, so they might not be able to give him a slot
every week on Breakfast. A prediction for you—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Oh.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a bit of a shame because I saw him on TV this morning and
when he was speaking to New Zealanders I fe lt my majority in the Rotorua electorate
going up. So I would like to keep him there. A plea to Breakfast and TVNZ: give him
some more time for the good of our majorities.
Here is a prediction for the next 3 years. In the next 3 years, when we have shown
New Zealanders that we have continued to work hard for them and deliver on the
commitments and promises we made to them  during this last election campaign when
they re-elected us to govern this country, I guarantee that when we get there and it is
time to consider John Key as Prime Minist er, his commitments to New Zealand and
New Zealanders, and the very hard work that  he and this Government has done on their
behalves, it will not be David Shearer on the ot her side that he is up against. There is
my prediction: David Shearer is gone from the Big Gay Out and dumped from
Breakfast, and I do not think it will be very long before he is finding another seat on that
side a row or two back. I wish him the ve ry best because he was quite a good cricket
player a year or so ago in Cambridge, but that is about all I remember of him. It is about
all that the people of Cambridge probably know about him as well. Where is Winston
Peters when we need a real Leader of the Opposition?
What I want to say is that these 3 y ears are about economic development for New
Zealand, something that was woefully lack ing over the 9 years of the last Labour
Government. We started under very difficult circumstances in the last 3 years, delivered
on every promise and every commitment we made as a party to New Zealanders, and
now we must focus. In roading we must  do more work. A great start—$12 billion
invested over 10 years. In the Bay of Plenty, a brand new road that will go from the Te
Puke area—the Te Puke bypass,  I call it—between Rotorua a nd Tauranga to the port
will cut out about 24 or 25 minutes from a retu rn journey. That is great if you want to
go and visit the beautiful part of the Bay of Plenty and the coastline or Tauranga and so
on, but it is important for our economy in that area of New Zealand, where we produce
a lot of trees and a lot of goods that go to th e port. That road will cut down the time it
takes for us to get our goods to the port. We therefore wi ll be more productive. When
we are more productive, we can be more competitive, and that will be more money back
into the Bay of Plenty. Roads of national significance are also an important part of that.
Broadband and communications—wonderful. La st year, before the election, they
started digging trenches in Rotorua a nd in 33 other towns and cities around New
Zealand for ultra-fast broadband. New Zealande rs cannot wait for this to happen and be
delivered, because for far too long we were left with inadequate ways to communicate
with the world and with each other. Rural broadband as well—$300 million the
Government will be investing into this. I was told by some of my constituents in a rural
area, where their cellphones have never wo rked under the 9 years of the previous
Labour Government, that a new tower is goi ng up, their cellphones will work, and they
will get internet coverage faster than actually  posting a letter. That was what it was like
before, under the Labour Governme nt, in rural areas: it was qu icker to post a letter and
508 Address in Reply 16 Feb 2012
get a response, sometimes. Rural broadband is  very important for us to reform our
economy and give us some of the advantages that we need so that we can grow.
Taking away red tape and bureaucracy—t he Resource Management Act. We
completed some significant reform there previously, but there is a lot more to do to free
up New Zealanders to get on with their live s and business, at the same time continuing
to protect our wonderful environment. Time is almost up. Can I say to those who have
come—

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Thank goodness.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: I will take a little bi t more if you want me to. Can I say to those
who have come to listen to maiden speeches  that you are very welcome here; this is
your House. It is great to see some friends  come and support our new MPs. As with all
colleagues on this side of the House, I look forward to the next 3 years of a John Key -
led National Government delivering for Ne w Zealanders and working hard for New
Zealanders. It is going to be an exciting 3 ye ars as we work towards a brighter future.
Kia ora. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Can I begin this Address
in Reply speech today in congratulating T odd McClay not just on that speech but
actually on the stunning result that was achieved in Rotorua, a seat that was previously
held by Labour. A big increase in his majo rity, over 7,400, and ac tually typical of
results right through provi ncial New Zealand, where that middle group of New
Zealanders strongly back the programme th at this Government has set down under the
leadership of John Key. Can I join other members and congratulate the new members of
this House. I am particularly proud to be he re as a National member and to see that new
generation coming through with National and a whole range of very, very talented
people coming into this Parliament to make  a contribution. The part that makes me
particularly proud as part of this National Government is the extent to which, on this
side of the House, there is an understanding of the challenges that face our country. I
have to say that I do worry that those on the opposite side of the House have no idea of
the challenges, economically, that our country faces, the problems that we have incurred
over the last decade, and the importance for th e future of our country that we get our
economy growing more strongly.
The Government in the Address in Reply debate has set out four really important
priorities in this term of Parliament about responsibly managing a Government’s
finances—about, as we saw today with th e Budget Policy Statement, getting New
Zealand books back into the black sooner and faster. When I look around the world, and
I see how many countries in the world are going to have their books in the black by
2014-15, there are very few, and I am proud to be part of this Government that is
achieving that. What surprises me is that in every question from Opposition members,
in every speech, I hear lots of promises about how they will spend more money, but
very little about how they will actually grow the economy, particularly the productive
sector. That is the only way in which we can secure the incomes, the jobs, and the
prosperity for the future.
There has also been a huge focus across the ministerial team around building a more
competitive and productive economy, and abou t building better public services, and I
want to talk about that in some detail with respect to my own portfolios. And, of course,
there is the huge challenge for this country and for this Parliament and Government of
rebuilding Christchurch, for which there is  such a strong commitment and for which I
pay tribute to the work of the Minister  for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Gerry
Brownlee, who I think every person in th is House acknowledges has got one of the
toughest jobs over the next 3 years.
16 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 509
A key part of the Government’s program me is about improving public services and
improving New Zealand’s productivity. I wa nt to talk for a moment about the
challenges in the local government sector. You see, one of the big co ncerns we have is
that the productive part of our economy has actually been in recession going all the way
back to 2002. If we look at our core exporting industries, we see that the extra costs and
impositions that were placed on them dur ing the term of the previous Labour
Government have seen those sectors stagnate , and the big areas of growth have been
both central and local government. I note, fo r instance, that over the last decade the
single biggest increase in co sts for households and businesse s has been the increase in
rates. For the last 10 years that increase ha s been at 6.85 percent per annum. That is
more than double the ra te of inflation, and I want to reflect on the changes that were
made in all the local government legislation in 2002.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What are you going to do about it?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I invite the member who is in terjecting to go back and read
the Hansard of what the Labour Government sa id at the time. What the Labour
Government said at the time was that those measures were actually going to generate
cost savings. They have done the opposite. Let me put it this way. If rate increases over
the last decade had been at the same level th ey had been for the previous decade, prior
to those changes Labour made, the New Zeal and annual rates bill would be a billion
dollars—a billion dollars—a year  less. What is more, if we talk in terms of households
that are under pressure in terms of their cost s and their standard of living, those changes
have brought about $500 a year  in increased rates for th e average household, over and
above what they would be if those rate increases had been  what they were through the
previous decade.
I want to challenge the member on a further concern, and that is in terms of the level
of debt within the local government sector. I have to say that debt is the issue of our
time, whether it be household debt, whether it be country debt, or whether it be debt
within local government. This Government has been successful—we have seen over the
last 2 years household debt come down after it burgeoned in the term of the previous
Labour Government, and what we have seen in terms of the farm sector is debt plateau
over the last 3 years. But although the Government has been successful my worry is that
over the same period we have seen local government debt not just go up but go up by
ever-increasing amounts. Since the Local Gove rnment Act changes that were made by
members opposite, we have seen local government debt quadruple from $2 billion to $8
billion and continuing to rise. So I say—a nd members on this side of the House say—
that ongoing growth in that debt is not right, and that it will compromise the capacity for
New Zealand to move forward and to be able to grow competitively.
The first thing we need to do, in response to the member’s question, is go back and
have a fresh look at those ch anges that Labour made to broaden the role of local
government. I say to the member opposite that  those changes that were made in 2002,
which imposed very large compliance costs on our councils and expa nded the role of
local government far more widely, have come with a very expensive cost for New
Zealand households and New Zealand busin esses, and that is something this
Government is looking to reform.
I also want to draw attention to what ha s occurred around wage costs. If we look at
the latest labour cost index, this is what it shows. [Interruption] If members would listen
they might learn something. Over the cour se of the last Labour Government labour
costs in the State sector and in the local government sector grew significantly faster than
they did in the private sector. What this G overnment has been succ essful in doing is
bringing back those increasing labour costs within those core Government agencies.
510 Address in Reply 16 Feb 2012
But what worries me is this. Over the la st 3 years the labour costs in the local
government sector have been increasing at mo re than double the ra te of those in the
central government sector. It is our view th at the same fiscal discipline that this
Government has brought to central government ’s books needs to be translated into the
local government sector so that we can get those efficiency gains. We actually need
both central and local government containing their costs. We need  central and local
government supporting those core productive in dustries that actually create the wealth
for this country, the jobs, and the future prospects we wish for in this country of ours.
The John Key - led Government over the last  3 years has shown that it is up to the
challenges that this country faces in very difficult times. What the Government has set
out in the Address in Reply debate is the changes we intend to make in a number of
sectors to improve the competitiveness of th is country. We as a close-knit team are
united in our wish to raise New Zealand’s liv ing standards and to provide the sort of
policies that will mean that this country is able to pros per and go forward. I am looking
forward this year to some of  those local government change s that can assist in that
bigger picture of making sure this country can be the best little country on earth.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: On the first occasion that I have spoken in Parliament
during this parliamentary term, can I ta ke the opportunity to congratulate you, Mr
Assistant Speaker Tisch, on your role, and all the team from the Speaker’s office. I look
forward to a rewarding year of debate under your direction. Can I also take the
opportunity to congratulate all returning members who have been elected to the House
again for this parliamentary term; I look forward to engaging with all returning
members in a high level of debate, because we  have many important issues in front of
us. I want to particularly congratulate th e new members of Parl iament. We have had
many fine maiden speeches already, and I look forward to the balance resuming this
afternoon.
I do want to say that the last three speak ers in this debate have been pretty
interesting. I think they have actually personified that arrogance of the second term of
the National-led Government. We have had Jonathan Coleman, Todd McClay, and Nick
Smith—the arrogance of this new National Go vernment personified. In fact, Dr Smith
spent much of his speech pouring scorn on the local bodies up and down this country,
and not telling us what he was prepared to  do about the problem he was identifying. Is
that not typical of the arrogance of Nationa l members? They identify the problems, say
it is all Labour’s fault, and do not have one plan or one specific id ea about what to do
