items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: We have heard the platitudes of  nearly every member in the
House, and along with those I add mine as we ll. My congratulations go to iwi, to the
Government, to the Public Serv ice, to the Office of Treaty Settlements, to Crown Law,
and to everybody involved in trying to bring closure to this aspe ct of New Zealand’s
history.
But let us not forget that it is a deal betw een the Crown and iwi. Therefore, I want to
ruffle a few feathers, as I am wont to do on many occasions, and say that this House
550 Ng āti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 16 Feb 2012
looks very seriously at how we deal with Tr eaty settlements. I say that because when
the bill comes to the M āori Affairs Committee, the sele ct committee cannot change any
part of the deal between iwi and the Crown—it cannot do that. And sometimes I wonder
why we waste iwi time, and why we waste the House’s time, by having the bill go to a
select committee. It is my opinion that because it is a deal between the Crown and iwi,
there must be some way where we can speed up the process so that iwi can get on with
the job of looking after iwi.
So I want to say that what we have done in the select committee is two things. One is
to split the committee in half and have  a couple of committees go out and do our
business. And we have also promised our selves that the tu rn-round will not be 6
months, it will not be 3 months ; it will be between 4 and 8 weeks. So we give that
commitment to iwi so that they can get on with the job at hand.
I will not be too long, but there is something else that I want to respond to, and that is
some suggestion that section 9 of the State- Owned Enterprises Act has something to do
with what we are talking about. All I can sa y is that at the end of the consultation
process, I can guarantee—because I am a member of this Government—that there will
be the Crown’s response to iwi and the Crown’s recognition that it must take into
account the Treaty of Waitangi. That is the Cr own’s responsibility. So if section 9 does
go, there will be a rewritten clau se that still says the Crown has a responsibility to take
into account the Treaty of Waitangi.
I just briefly want to mention somethi ng that the Hon Parekura Horomia mentioned
in his speech, and that is the issue about  rates, and it has been a vexed issue for
Government as far back as my great-grandfat her who just happened to be a member of
Parliament nearly 100 years ago. I think that there is coming a time where we will—
both sides of the House—have to agree on a mechanism for the rating, or not, of M āori
land, because it is getting completely out of hand, and the only losers are those M āori
who have shares in Māori land.
Hoi anō, taku mihi ki a koutou katoa. An ō taku mihi ki a ng ā rangatira o te Whare
nei, taku tuakana a Parekura, ā, n ō reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, kia ora mai t ātou
katoa.
[Thus I acknowledge you all. My compliments to the leading figures of this House, to
my elder Parekura, so greetings to you, greetings to you, and greetings to us all.]

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker
Robertson, ng ā mihi tino pai o t ēnei tau. T ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou ng ā
rangatira o Ngai T āmanuhiri me Ng āti Mākino. Ko koutou te reo karanga o te r ā. Mihi
tonu atu ki a koutou katoa, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Roberts on, and the very finest of this year to you.
Greetings to you, th e leaders of Ngai T āmanuhiri and Ng āti M ākino, greetings. It is
your voice that calls today. This acknowledgmen t is directed at you all, so salutations
and greetings.]
I am very proud to join with my Labour co lleagues here in support of the two bills
before this House this evening: the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill and the
Ngāti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill. It is an  honour, because I completed my maiden
speech just a couple of days ago and today is my first official speech before the House,
so I am very thrilled to be talking to these very important bills.
I acknowledge Ngai T āmanuhiri and Ng āti M ākino for travelling here today to
celebrate this significant occasion and the pa ssage of these important bills before the
House, and in the progression of your Treaty settlements. So I mihi to you all.
As an uri of Tahup ōtiki—Ngāi Tahu—I would like to specifi cally just focus at this
point of my speech on the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill. I acknowledge the
whanaungatanga connections that  I have and that all of us in Te Tai Tonga and Ng āi
16 Feb 2012 Ngāti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 551
Tahu wh ānui, whom I represent,  have with Ngai T āmanuhiri. I acknowledge the
common ancestry we that we have as cousins. The Ngai T āmanuhiri claims settlement
is the first of the T ūranga claims, which is the first in the Gisborne area. So I also
acknowledge getting first off the blocks in term s of the progression of  this bill to this
stage. I look forward to seeing other progress made across the Tūranga region.
We would not be here today without the support, effort, hard work, and toil over
many years that has gone into the claims from both of the respective iwi. I acknowledge
all of those who have gone before—who ha ve progressed and championed and gone
through tribunal processes, and the hard sw eat and toil that goe s into bringing the
settlements to this point in time. In partic ular, I would like to acknowledge all of those
who were involved in the Ngai T āmanuhiri lands claim negotiations team: Dawn
Pōmana, Reuben Riki, who died just before  the land claims hearings commenced,
Melanie Tarsau, and Pauline Hill; then, in 2007, Hope T ūpara; and from 2008 to 2011,
Nā Rongowhakaata Raih ānia. I also acknowledge the research team that was involved
with the Ngai Tāmanuhiri claims: Warren Pōhatū, Noel Pōhatū, Hope Tūpara, kaumātua
Nā Raihānia, Hare P ōhatū, who is deceased, Rose Thompson, who is also deceased—
and we acknowledge them—Tem ple Isaacs, and Nolan Raih ānia, who I understand are
in the House tonight. I acknowledge all of those individuals in regard to participating in
the hard work of advancing th ese important claims through to this point in time, to this
stage of the bill.
In terms of my own association with Ngai T āmanuhiri, I would like to relate my own
firsthand experience dealing with Ngai T āmanuhiri when I was with Ng āi Tahu. I
mentioned the close association that we ha ve whakapapa-wise, and that extended right
in terms of the fisheries settlements, with  the Treaty tribes coal ition, and the kaupapa
that we stood on with mana whenua, ma na moana. So I acknowledge Ngai T āmanuhiri
in that respect and in the history that we have  in those other areas of Treaty settlements.
In particular, what I learnt from my associations with Ng āi T āmanuhiri—and, in
particular, Dawn P ōmana—was the very principled approach that they have to their
tikanga. That was to the fore in all the dealings that Ng āi Tahu had with Ngai
Tāmanuhiri in terms of our annual dealings around our fisheries tr ansactions and the
like. That has flowed through to all of the mahi that has gone on, culminating this
evening in the presentation of this bill for its first reading.
I would like to also acknowledge the history that is embodied in the settlement that is
now before us in this bill, which was ra tified through the deed of settlement. That
actually goes back to all of the historical in justices and grievances that were inflicted
upon Ngai T āmanuhiri by the Crown, right through from the 1860s, in terms of land
dealings and the operation of the Povert y Bay Commission, and the impact of the
operation of the Native Land Court. There is a lot of history and a lot of grievances
there, and they were fully expressed through the Waitangi Tribunal reports. They
highlighted the very severe breaches of the Treaty in the Tūranga area and, in particular,
against Ngai Tāmanuhiri.
The historical background is there, and these settlements go some way towards trying
to acknowledge the grievances of the pa st, and I know the Crown does include its
apologies, but it does not nearly compensate for all of the lost opportunities, the mamae,
and the grievance that has been inflicted upon the iwi and the ma ny generations of
whānau. That is why I am very proud to be here this evening to play my part in
advancing this important bill through to the next stage, so we can actually enact some
measure of redress and compen sation and apologies through th is legislation, and so we
can address the issues of the past and also  lay a platform for ongoing relationships for
Ngai Tāmanuhiri and the Crown, and also for Ngāti Mākino and the Crown.
552 Ng āti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 16 Feb 2012
I would just like to support again with my Labour colleagues the passage of this
legislation through to the select committ ee stage. I acknowledge my whanaunga the
Hon Tau Henare nō te nōta as our chair of the M āori Affairs Committee. I look forward
to playing my part on the committee, especi ally when we will be breaking into two
subcommittees so we can advance the progression of these bills, and to leading this
legislation right through this House so that we can finally put the seal on it and pass it
right the way through the House. I commend the passage of this legislation at this time.
Kia ora anō tātou katoa.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I am pleased to speak on the Ngai
Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill and the Ngāti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill. I must
admit to the House this is the first time I have spoken on a Treaty settlement bill. I am
new on the M āori Affairs Committee, so I apologise to those listening if I cannot give
this legislation quite the thorough e xplanation, acknowledgment, and indeed
acclamation that I know the legislation deserv es. I will, however, be doing my best to
listen to the submissions to the M āori Affairs Committee, and I am sure I will indeed
get quite an education under the guidance of rangatira Tau Henare, our chairman on the
Māori Affairs Committee.
I wish to first acknowledge the work that has been done by the Minister for Treaty of
Waitangi Negotiations, the Hon Chris Finlayson, and all those involved in getting these
settlement bills to the point that they are at now. The great progress that the Minister has
made on completing final and durable settle ments of Treaty of Waitangi claims in a
timely manner, through his tenure as the Mini ster for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations,
is impressive.
I think New Zealand is still maturing as a nation, and we are stepping forward into
the 21st century. Part of the maturing process is acknowledging the rights and wrongs of
the past. It would be easy for New Zealanders  to simply ignore that in our short history
as a country many cultural and economic wrongs were committed. Indeed, for many
decades New Zealand has ignored that these is sues prevailed. But the fact that we are
here together, today, debating these bills, th ese pieces of legisla tion, that will stand
alongside many past and future settlement bills , indicates that as a country we are ready
to accept the past and move forward.
The part of the country that I represen t, the Botany electora te, is predominantly
white, middle to upper-class suburban Auckland. It is an area of the country that is quite
sceptical of Treaty settlements, and I have  to admit that I probably was too, up until
recently. But the more I have seen and read  of Treaty settlements and the programme,
and the more I have watched from afar the work that the Minister and the Office of
Treaty Settlements have done, the more I can  see that through reso lving the wrongs of
the past we can refloat and regain moment um for the waka that is harmonious New
Zealand race relations. In my view the key part to reassuring Ne w Zealanders who are
sceptical about Treaty settleme nts is to assure them that  under this Government Treaty
settlements have been, and will continue to be, full, fair, and final.
Parts of the deeds of settlement, which out line historical grievances for both Ngai
Tāmanuhiri and Ng āti M ākino, I have to say, make for ve ry sobering reading. In the
case of Ngai T āmanuhiri we read of indisc riminate looting of the T ūranga region at the
hands of the Crown in the aftermath of th e Waerenga-a-hika attack. The Waerenga-a-
hika attack itself saw women and childre n, among other occupants, put through
unwarranted and unjust attacks at the ha nds of the Crown. Land was compulsorily
acquired without compensation, and many Ngai Tāmanuhiri were left virtually landless.
A similar story is told in the case of Ngāti Mākino. The year 1864 saw the loss of life
at the hands of the Crown, confiscation of la nd in the Eastern Bay of Plenty took place
in 1866, and between 1873 and 1900, 82,000 hectares of Ng āti M ākino land was
16 Feb 2012 Ngāti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 553
alienated. By the end of the 19 th century less than 4 percent of land of Ng āti Mākino’s
Waitahanui, T āhunaroa, and Whakarewa blocks rema ined in their hands—and please
excuse my pronunciation if I have got any of those incorrect. These are just a few of the
many injustices that took place in the past—injustices that up until recently were not
acknowledged. But the Crow n has now acknowledged thes e injustices and has
apologised through these two settlements. The settlements we have before us tonight
will help Ngai T āmanuhiri and Ng āti Mākino unlock economic potential and provide a
boost to their regional and provi ncial areas. In turn, these two iwi will be able to
contribute in an even greater way toward s building a more competitive and productive
New Zealand economy.
These bills are worthy of passage through th eir first reading toni ght. I ask that the
House does support them, and I hope that we have thorough and good quality
recognition of the issues through the select  committee process. I am looking forward to
hearing about the issues that we will be discussing at the select committee, and I look
forward to this legislation passing its first reading.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call, 5 minutes with Labour and 5 minutes w ith the Greens. I will ring a bell with 1
minute to go.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker Tisch. Ka t āpiri atu āku mihi i waihotia ki a koutou Ng āti M ākino, Ngai
Tāmanuhiri i tau mai nei ki roto i t ō Whare, ki te whakarongo ki ēnei kōrero i tēnei pō.
Nō reira tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch. I add  my tributes that were bestowed upon
you Ngāti Mākino and Ngai T āmanuhiri when you landed here  in your House to listen
to these speeches tonight. So greetings to you collectively, greetings to you and to us
all.]
Treaty settlements are more than an academic  exercise. It is about passion and the
history of people who are trying to seek redress for past wrongs. I want to acknowledge
that this is a first reading opportunity for the bills from Ngai T āmanuhiri and Ng āti
Mākino to come to the House, so the subs tance of the investig ations on the Ngai
Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill and the Ng āti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill will in
fact occur in the M āori Affairs Committee, which is right . But it is important to note
that in the innovation of hearing Treaty se ttlements over this period of time—and I
came into Parliament when the first lot of Tr eaty settlements started to come to this
House—we as members of Parliament have  started to improve processes around the
processing of Treaty settlements, because, by  and large, if the purpose of Brendan
Horan’s speech was to highlight that the nation that we seek to create is one built
strongly on biculturalism, and the national anthem is in M āori and English, then Treaty
settlements are an important part of cr eating a sense of nationhood and identity, and
addressing the historical wrongs is a strong pillar of what Aotearoa New Zealand should
stand for. It is a country where those rights of tangata whenua are recognised, where the
hurts of the past are addressed, but where, enab led to get over that particular hurdle, the
next generation can look forward and move forward with confidence. And it is no easy
feat to reach this part of a Treaty settlement. So my comments are, by and large, to both
Ngāti Mākino and Ngai Tāmanuhiri.
Sometimes people wonder why we are coming to  the House to hear the first reading
speeches when everybody seems to be saying the same thing again, and again, and again
in 10 different ways. But let me give you three good reasons why the select committee
process is an important proce ss. Firstly, it ensures the intent of your deed aligns to how
the legislation actually reads. As you all know, some times the devil is in the detail. So
it is really important during the scrutiny at th e select committee for members to look at
554 Ng āti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 16 Feb 2012
what was intended in the deed and how the legislation reads to  ensure that it lines up.
That is the first thing.
The second thing is the broader aspect  of educating our country. Members of
Parliament hold, in some sense, a microcos m of the view of our communities, from
where we come from, and we can inform our communities about what is happening
through the Treaty settlement process, an d allay fears, but also present new
opportunities for people to learn about historie s that are not easily found in the history
books.
The third part of the select committee process, which is of ten a critical part but the
most difficult to challenge and change, is for members or Parliament to put greater
scrutiny on the way in which the Crown or the Government acts, and that is through the
Office of Treaty Settlements when it deals with M āori. It is very difficult to challenge
the way in which the Office of Treaty Settlements often engages through the negotiation
process, but it is an opp ortunity for members of Parliament  to put a fine lens on issues
that are highlighted to them at the select  committee process to ensure that people are
treated fairly in the way they  seek to negotiate  redress through their Treaty settlement.
So those are but three reasons why the select committee process in bringing your bills to
the House is a necessary if  not absolutely important task of achieving Treaty
settlements.
I will reserve my comments on the substa nce of these two bills, if I get the
opportunity to speak to the th ird readings. But I want to  acknowledge those people who
have passed, both from Ng āti M ākino and Ngai T āmanuhiri, those people who have
carried the flame of your Treaty settlemen t claim to this point, and those kaum ātua who
now hold the flame so that the next generati on continues to tell the story that must be
told to ensure the most important clause of  both your bills—and that is clause 4: “This
Act binds the Crown.” And for as long as this  Act binds the Crown, then it is inherent
on every member of Parliament who accedes to your Treaty settle ment that it be
implemented in the manner for which it was intended, and that is to uphold the deed in
your Treaty settlement.
Nō reira, i raro i ērā kupu poto kua whakar āpopoto āku nei kōrero ki a koutou. T ēnā
koutou katoa.
[So under the realm of those brief words, I shorten this address of mine to you
collectively. Greetings to you all.]

Denise Roche. My apologies—there are three of you who look very similar.

items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. We P ākehā often
look the same! T ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, tēnā koutou. E ng ā rangatira o Ng āti Mākino
nau mai, haere mai ki konei. E ng ā rangatira o Ngai T āmanuhiri, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā

[Greetings to you collectively, greetings, greetings. Welcome to the leaders of Ng āti

This is my first time as well, standing after my maiden speech, and I am privileged to
be speaking on these bill s tonight, the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill and the
Ngāti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill. I acknowledge all the statements that have gone
before me, and I particularly want to mi hi to Nanaia Mahuta about the building of
nationhood and the importance of the passing of  these settlements, which will do that
for our country of Aotearoa.
The Green Party has a story that we want to tell. It is basically about our relationship
with Ngai T āmanuhiri. This is not to disrespect the settlement process that is going
through for Ng āti M ākino, but there has been a personal relationship that we want to
16 Feb 2012 Ngāti Mākino & Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bills 555
outline. The $12 million settlement can be de scribed really as a deal, but not a
settlement. The people from Muriwai and the rohe katoa have negotiated a deal, and we
have been told by some that it was a valuab le process in terms of reaffirming their own
story, but it is a deal. It is what they c ould get. Settlement means when all the dust has
been laid to rest; there is still dust floating in the clouds around Te Kur ī a Paoa. It is not
for the Green Party to say what should have been included in that settlement—that is
your story; that is the work that you have been doing for decades and decades—but we
do have a story that we want to acknowledge.
Ngai Tāmanuhiri say that when Capitain C ook’s and Young Nick’s ship entered the
bay at T ūranga-nui-a-Kiwa they became the front line of the historical mythology of
how this country was colonised. Their maunga—Te Kur ī a Paoa—was renamed Young
Nicks Head by Captain Cook. Th e appropriation of Te Kur ī a Paoa did not stop there,
and that is how the Green Party, through my colleague Catherine Delahunty and her
partner Gordon Jackman, became involved, supporting the 21 st century struggle of Ngai
Tāmanuhiri to stop the sale of Te Kur ī a Paoa to a New York stockbroker called John
Griffin.
The maunga had been in Pākehā hands for many years as a farm, and when the Coop
family decided to sell it Ngai T āmanuhiri sought desperately for the money to make an
offer to regain their maunga. In 2002 the Gr eens supported their occupation of the p ā
site Rangihoua, and Green MPs at the time Rod Donald, Nandor Tanczos, and our co-
leader Metiria Turei all vi sited the occupation, if you can call sitting on your own
maunga such a thing. Current Green MP Catherine Delahunty and Gordon Jackman also
supported the Ngai T āmanuhiri h īkoi to Wellington to fight  for the opportunity for
purchase. A ghastly compromise meant that some of the w āhi tapu would be kept as
public land and access to them acknowledged, while most of the maunga was sold to Mr
Griffin. Foreign ownership of an iconic landm ark was a national disgrace, as well as a
breach of te Tiriti, but Mr Griffin had the most money. Under this bill, Ngai Tāmanuhiri
regain the pā site on the maunga, Rangihoua, and the cl iff-face is gifted to the nation in
recognition of history. Their generosity is gr eater than anything ever shown to you as a
people in this painful story, but the pā site is an important and significant inclusion.
The Green Party still believes that foreign ownership of sacred maunga is an abuse of
te Tiriti, and we regret that the settlement process amounts to a partial redress of a deep
hara. The access to fighting grounds of an cient value and current needs is via the
permission of the American stockbroker and his farm manager—it is goodwill. It is
good that the forestry lands on Wharerata wi ll be available to purchase now to Ngai
Tāmanuhiri, but at market rates. We stole your whenua and now you can buy it back at
market rates—that is the deal. Take it or leave it!
There is more to be said on this history, but at first reading we simply wish to
acknowledge the people of Muriwai, the rohe, and also Te Kur ī a Paoa, where the pou
was placed by the people during the protests and where it still stands in the winds,
always belonging to mana whenua, whatever the outcome of the process. And so it will
always stand. We acknowledge the journey that you have yet to go. We will support this
bill. We recognise that it does not meet the full redress, and that is something we are
concerned about, but we support you. N ō reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou
katoa.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakaw ā. Tēnā koe e
te Whare. Rau rangatira m ā, tēnei te mihi ki a koutou i runga i te kaupapa o te r ā. Tēnā
koutou ngā rangatira o Ngai T āmanuhiri me Ng āti Mākino. Tēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou,

[Greetings to you, Mr Assistant Speaker Ti sch, and the House. I extend greetings to

Ngai Tāmanuhiri and Ng āti Mākino. Greetings to you, gree tings to you, and greetings

I am proud to stand and take the final call in this first reading of the Ngai Tāmanuhiri
Claims Settlement Bill and the Ng āti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill, and very proud of
the record that we have made as a Nationa l Government in getting durable settlements
through, as part of our progress towards fu ll partnership. I am pr oud of our Ministers
involved, and, like all members of this H ouse, I am very proud to be supporting

Waiata.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: As the lead speaker on
these cognate bills covering five iwi, I seek  leave for an extension of 2 minutes on my
time.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
there any objection? There is no objection. I shall ring the bell at 10 minutes with 2
minutes to go.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Tēnā koe. I move, That the Ng āti Manawa and Ng āti
Whare Claims Settlement Bill, Nga Wa i o Maniapoto (Waipa River) Bill, Ng āti
Pāhauwera Treaty Claims Settlement Bill, and Ngati Porou Claims Settlement Bill be
now read a second time.
Nā reira tuatahi, kei te mihi at u ki a koutou kua hara mai nei i t ēnei pō me ng ā mea
kāre an ō kia tae mai. E tika ana kia mihi atu ki ēnei iwi, ā, kua h īkoi i te h īkoi te
roroanga mai i te t īmatanga tae noa ki t ēnei rangi, n ā reira, t ēnā koutou e kaha ākina.
Tēnā koutou i ō koutou tini aitu ā. Ka hoki aku mahara ki a t ātou e t ū kaha ana ki te
tautoko i ēnei āhuatanga kai roto i ō koutou iwi. Ko Bill Bird t ētahi, ko te p āpā
Whatumoana, ko T ā Hēnare Ngāta, ko Meagan Joe, ko r ātau me ng ā mate o te w ā nei.
Haere koutou, okioki mai.
Nā reira, ka hoki au ki t ēnei kōrero, ka mihi atu ki a koutou kua rauika i te p ō nei.
Kāre e roa aku kōrero mō ēnei pire nā te mea he pānuitanga tuarua tēnei, ā, waiho mō te
pānui whakamutunga, te pānui tuatoru kia tū motuhake ēnei pire, ā, e āta kōrero ai tātau
i konei i roto i te Whare Pāremata. Heoi anō, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou.
[Firstly, I wish to acknowledge those of you who came this evening and also those
who have not yet arrived. It is  appropriate that I pay tribute to these tribes who have
been on this long journey since the beginni ng to this day. Congratulations on your
resilience. I acknowledge you and your m any dead. My thoughts go back to when we
stood staunch in support of these circumstances  within your tribes. Bill Bird was one,
our father-figure Whatumoana, Sir H ēnare Ngata, and Meagan Joe were others, and
the deaths of the day. Depart, rest there.

items.speaker: So I go back to this comment
items.text: welcome to you collectively who have assembled here
tonight. I will not spend too long on these bi lls, because it is the second reading. Wait
for the final and third reading when these bi lls stand independently and when we can
address them here at length in  the Chamber. So greetings to  you, greetings to you, and
greetings to you.]
16 Feb 2012 Second Readings 557

items.speaker: Ngāti Manawa
items.text: the area of interest for Ng āti Manawa is based around Murupara and
the Kaingaroa Plains in the inland Bay of Plenty. The claims of Ng āti Manawa relate
primarily to the consequences of its loyalty to the Crown during the New Zealand Wars,
Crown actions and omissions in respect of the operation and impact  of the native land
laws, and the Crown’s land purchasing techni ques, particularly in respect of land Ng āti
Manawa. This settlement is intended to recognise the traditional, historical, cultural, and
spiritual interests of Ngāti Manawa. The key aspects of Ngāti Manawa’s cultural redress
package aim to reinvigorate the relationship between Ng āti Manawa and sites of
significance. It is the intention of this se ttlement that this will be done through the
vesting of sites of particular significance to Ng āti Manawa, the erection of pou r āhui to
mark traditional iwi boundaries, th e creation of a body to restore Ng āti Manawa’s and
Ngāti Whare’s mana over their ancestral river and their relationship with tuna, and the
transfer and gift back of the ancestral maunga, Tāwhiuau, to Ngāti Manawa.

items.speaker: Mō Ngāti Whare
items.text: the claims of Ng āti Whare primarily relate to the Crown’s actions
during the New Zealand Wars, specifically the impact of the Native Land Court and
subsequent land alienation, the enactment of  the Urewera District Native Reserve Act
1896, which disenfranchised Ng āti Whare from its land, a nd the return of Minginui
Village by the Crown without providing Ng āti Whare with sufficient resources to bring
the village infrastructure up to the standards of the Government. Ng āti Whare’s
settlement acknowledges the Whirinaki Te Pua- ā-Tāne Conservation Park as a special
place to both Ngāti Whare as kaitiaki and the people of New Zealand. It also establishes
a renewed and enduring partnership between Ngāti Whare and the Crown. In particular,
the settlement provides for a joint governance of the Whirinaki Te Pua- ā-Tāne
Conservation Park by Ng āti Whare and the Crown. The settlement also provides Ng āti
Whare with assistance to regenerate indigenous mata ī, rimu, and kahikatea in areas of
pine forest within the Whirinaki Crown forest licensed land.
The Nga Wai o Maniapoto (Waipa River) Bill: an ō, ka mihi au ki a koutou o
Maniapoto. I acknowledge the work carried out by the M āori Affairs Committee and
thank committee members for their support a nd guidance on the Nga Wai o Maniapoto
(Waipa River) Bill. The relationship between Ng āti Maniapoto and the Waip ā River is
significant and enduring, based on a deep -felt respect that  the people of Ng āti
Maniapoto have for the river Waip ā. This gives rise to their responsibility to protect te
mana o te wai and to exercise kaitiak itanga in accordance with their tikanga. Ng āti
Maniapoto and Waikato-Tainui  share a strong relationshi p through the Tainui waka,
which is manifested in the s upport they each give to the K īngitanga. In a similar way,
their sacred awa, Waikato and Waip ā, are inextricably linked. From Ng āruawāhia, the
pathways of these rivers join, and their wa ters flow together as one. The overarching
purpose of the co-governance and co-management arrangements is to restore and
maintain the quality and integrity of the waters  that flow into and from, and form part
of, the Waip ā River for present and future generations. The co-governance
arrangements within the bill extend towards the headwaters of the Waip ā River at
Pekepeke Springs in the Rangitoto ranges, supporting the ongoing aspirations and
responsibilities shared by Ng āti Maniapoto and the Crown to  protect and nurture the
Waipā River. Extending the co-governance framework to include the whole of the
Waipā River will contribute significantly to achieving an integrated, holistic, and
coordinated approach to the management of both the Waip ā River and the Waikato
River, to the implementation of the vision and strategy, and to river rehabilitation and
clean-up initiatives. The Nga Wai o Mania poto (Waipa River) Bill complements the
Waikato River settlement and the Waik ato River co-management deeds with Ng āti
Tūwharetoa, Raukawa, and Te Arawa River Iw i. These arrangements are similar and
contribute to establishing a single, unified co-governance framework for both the Waipā
River and the Waikato River.
558 Second Readings 16 Feb 2012

items.speaker: The Ngati Porou Claims Settlement Bil l
items.text: the grievances of Ngati Porou are
longstanding. This bill recognises and addr esses those grievances and settles the
historical Treaty of Waitangi claims of Ngati Porou. The area of interest for Ngati Porou
is on the East Coast of the North Island. The hi storical grievances of Ngati Porou relate
primarily to the Crown’s fa ilure to honour its Treaty prom ise to respect Ngati Porou
rangatiratanga over its own affairs. The Crown imposed land tenure reform on Ngati
Porou, which deprived iwi members of collec tive control over thei r land and made it
difficult to utilise their land for economic development. Although it is not possible to
fully compensate Ngati Porou or any clai mant group for the loss that people have
suffered, the redress in this bill seeks to recognise the longstanding cultural and spiritual
association that Ngati Porou has within the regi on. It gives effect to the undertakings by
the Crown in the deed of settlement by offe ring reconciliation re dress, including an
agreed historical account, Crown acknowle dgments, and an apology; cultural redress
that vests sites of cultural and historic significance; and a number of arrangements
designed to facilitate good working relations hips between Ngati Porou and the Crown.
The financial and commercial redress of the settlement comprises $90 million in
financial and commercial redress, $20 million in  cultural and historical redress, and
redress over Crown properties,  including licensed forest la nd. I am confident that the
Ngati Porou Claims Settlement Bill will settle the claims of Ngati Porou in a full and
final manner, and set the foundation for a productive future relationship with the Crown.
Finally, I will speak on the Ng āti P āhauwera Treaty Claims Settlement Bill.
Although I was unable to participate in  the policy decisions about the Ng āti Pāhauwera
settlement, due to a declared conflict of interest—yeah—it is with great interest that I
stand to speak today in the second reading of the bill. Ng āti P āhauwera is a
confederation of hap ū with historical interests in nor thern Hawke’s Bay. The core area
of interest extends from south of Wairoa along the coastline to the Waikari River, inland
from these areas towards the Maungaharuru Ra nge, and north towards the Waiau River.
The claims of Ngāti Pāhauwera include the failure of the Crown to make sure that Ngāti
Pāhauwera had sufficient lands for its futu re needs during the process of the land
alienation that began in the 1850s. By the mid - 20th century Ng āti P āhauwera was
virtually landless, and ever since has suffered economic, social, and cultural
impoverishment. During the New Zealand Wa rs the Crown ignored warnings of a
possible attack on Ngāti Pāhauwera communities at Mōhaka. When the attack occurred,
the Crown provided minimu m assistance to help Ng āti P āhauwera recover from the
attack on the p ā and k āinga, even though the area had been  left virtually defenceless
because the warriors from Ngāti Pāhauwera were away with the Crown’s forces.
This bill seeks to right the wrongs of the past by recognising what has happened
through an agreed historical account, Cr own acknowledgments and an apology by the
Crown to Ng āti P āhauwera, and an acceptance by Ng āti P āhauwera of that apology.
This bill seeks to recognise the longstanding cultural and spiritual association that Ngāti
Pāhauwera has in the region, through vesting Te Heru o Tūreia in Ngāti Pāhauwera, and
the subsequent gift of a major portion of th at area to the people of New Zealand as a
historic reserve. Ngāti Pāhauwera will also retain Nakunaku as a historic reserve, and 14
other cultural redress properties will be invested in the iwi.
The bill also provides for some aspects of commercial redress to compensate Ng āti
Pāhauwera for what has been lost, including au thorising the transfer of five former
Wairoa District Council properties to Ng āti P āhauwera and licensed land within
Mōhaka Forest, as well as a right  of first refusal over Crown properties in the core area.
I am confident that the Ng āti P āhauwera Treaty Claims Sett lement Bill will settle the
iwi’s Treaty claims in a full and final manner. The redress provided to Ng āti Pāhauwera
can never compensate it for what has been lo st. I trust that the agreement reached with
16 Feb 2012 Second Readings 559
Ngāti Pāhauwera that is embodied in this bill will enhance the relationship between the
Crown and Ngāti Pāhauwera in the future.
I look forward to all these bills proceedi ng to the Committee stage without delay.
Ngā mihi ki a koutou kua hara mai nei i te pō nei, ā, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kei raro.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the next
speaker, I wish to advise the House that it is a split call between the Hon Shane Jones
and the Hon Parekura Horomia.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: I te tuatahi me mihi wh ānui atu ki ō tātou huanga,
ō tātou mātua whakarauika mai ki Te Ūpoko o te Ika ki roto i “t e ana o te raiona”. E
kara mā koutou nō Te Tai R āwhiti, ahakoa kōwhiti noa atu ng ā marama noho tonu mai
ana koutou i waenga n ōki i a m ātou nā reira, e kara e koa ana te ng ākau. Tēnā koutou
ngā kanohi pakeke, huri noa ki ng ā iwi e whai pānga ana ki ēnei kerēme, meinga nei ko
Ngāti Whare, Ng āti Manawa, ō tātou huanga i te taihau āuru i roto i te whare t ātai o
Maniapoto, huri atu ki te whitinga o te r ā, Ngāti Pāhauwera, Ngati Porou, t ēnā koutou.
Ēhara koutou i te iwi tauh ōu ki t ēnei Whare. Otir ā ko t āku he mihi atu ki a koutou.
Tautoko hoki i te reo, atu i t ō tātou Minita ki a koutou, ki a t ātou, nā, te menemene mai
ai koutou ki ng ā Māori katoa i roto i t ēnei Whare, kaua ki t ā koutou k ōtiro a H ēkia
anakenake. Nā reira, tēnā tātou katoa.
[An extensive welcome in the first inst ance to our relations and parents gathered
here in Wellington, in “the den of the lions ”. Those friends from the East Coast, you
have remained there amongst us for many m onths, we are really  pleased about that.
Acknowledgments to you, the adu lt faces and those tribes with interests in these claims,
Ngāti Whare, Ng āti Manawa, our relatives to the we st in the ance stral house of
Maniapoto, turning to the pl ace where the sun rises, Ng āti P āhauwera and Ngati
Porou, greetings to you collectively. You are no strangers to this House, and I welcome
you sincerely. I also endorse the sentiments expressed by our Minister to you and us
collectively. So cast a smile upon all the M āori members in this House, and not just
upon your girl, Hēkia, alone. Greetings to us all.]
I rise to make a short cont ribution. What we have ended up doing here is an unusual
innovation in terms of the rules of Parliament . We have been able to conflate several
bills into one session. I am told  that it is an initiative know n as a cognate. A cognate, as
you know, is something very familiar to the M āori people because it means your blood,
your whakapapa.
It is good to see that after a long period of  time we are finally seeing the end of the
Treaty settlement process fo r these particular tribes. Sir Doug Graham made his
contribution. We made our contribution, and I will be the first to admit that it could
have been improved upon. Dr Cullen—that peer less parliamentarian—towards the end
of our time certainly sped things up, so we have got no hesitation whatsoever in
supporting the current Minister for Treaty of  Waitangi Negotiations to expedite the
claims.
I think it is important that  we remind those of our m ātua and supporters from the
various iwi who are here this evening that there are other issues confronting you, not the
least of which those who have vested in terests in the ongoing administration and
utilisation of rivers and waters associated. That  is a big issue that stands in front of us.
But please do not make an unsubstantia ted, bare, politic al plea that M āoris own the
water. Please be sophisticated enough to bring back evidence and bring back claims that
bear strength that we have vested inte rests in the future in the rivers of P āhauwera, and
the rivers of Ngati Porou, and the rivers of  Maniapoto that cannot  be misconstrued or
abused, as we suffered the last time when David Garrett was here and sought to make
fun of the Waiwaia Accord when this legisl ation went through its first reading. I took a
little pleasure in reminding him, after he  made those foul remarks—completely
gratuitous—about the Maniapoto and Tainui people, that it was not long after that that a
560 Second Readings 16 Feb 2012
kēhua leapt out of the depths of  that water and swept him from this House. So bear that
in mind; these matters of Treaty and M āori spirituality are not to be trifled with. I must,
myself, remember to do as I say, and not just talk about it.
On the elements to do with Ngati Porou, we  have two senior members of the Ngati
Porou tribe—at least two—and a young man over there with his whakapapa from Ngati
Porou. I think those of us from the north often thought that the tribe that learnt best how
to deal with successive Governments was Ngati Porou, but when I look at the handsome
settlement the Arawas have walked away w ith, they have not done too bad themselves.
Unfortunately the truculent spirit that pervades the Ng āpuhi tends to keep them at the
margin, but time will tell whether or not the missionary spirit of goodwill and peace will
ever rise to the top of the Ngāpuhi political psyche. But that is for another night.
This is an evening when small tribes such as Ngāti Whare, Ngāti Manawa, in obscure
parts of Aotearoa, Ng āti P āhauwera with their long-vested interests in their river, and
Maniapoto, one of our largest iwi, with that he roic and very rich heritage of resistance
and providing, indeed, security for Te Kooti, in his time, and T āwhiao, are making
progress on this particular pa rt of their claim, the Waip ā River. So I join with my
colleagues in not only wishing the supporters well but reminding them, when we take it
to the next stage, please do not look for us, your Māori MPs, to uncritically support calls
that we own the water, without a substa ntial and robust basis for us not only to
prosecute that claim but to s ecure the endorsement of our P ākehā fellow citizens. T ēnā
tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Tautokotia atu ng ā
mihimihi ki a koe, t ēnā koe. Ki te Minita m ō te M ātauranga, te whanaunga e H ēkia, e
mihi kau ana, tēnā koe.
[I endorse the acknowledgments to you, gree tings. To the Minister of Education, the
relative Hēkia, I really acknowledge you, greetings.]
I was glad that my learned colleague from the n ōta did not say that Ngati Porou was
obscure, because it is paradise, and I certainly  do not bow from my vested interest. But
in recognising that, the role th at we play, I certainly want to  mihi to the hard work of
our pakeke and leaders of Ngati Porou, Apir ana Mahuika and Co., fo r that hard period
going through. And there have been tensions ; there is no doubt about it. I know most
other iwi do not have tensions and ructions, but we are honest people, we have tensions,
but we get through them, and for that I certainly want to commend our mātua Api.
E mihi kau ana i a koutou o Maniapoto. E roaroa atu te k ōrero mō te wai, mai i te
tīmata o ngā kerēme mō te wai. E rongo atu ki te k ōrero o te Shane nei m ō te āhua o te
wai. E mihi kau ana i a koutou. Kei a Nanaia te k ōrero m ō Maniapoto. I a koutou o
Ngāti Whare e mihi kau ana, t ēnā koutou. E pai atu ki te kite atu i a koutou. E
mokemoke noa iho e kore e konei a Bill, t ērā tangata e whai kaha ia tau, ia marama m ō
te take nei. Nō reira, tēnā koutou.
[I welcome you of Maniapoto. The conversa tion about water since the claims for
water began has been a lengthy one. I note the comments by Shane here in respect of
the water. But I really ack nowledge you collectively. Nanai a has the talk in regard to
Maniapoto. So to you of Ng āti Whare, I acknowle dge you, as well, greetings. It is
wonderful to see you, but I am bereft at the same time that Bill, that man who worked
hard each year and month for this matter, is no longer here. So greetings to you,
collectively.]
It is good to see that Ngāti Whare have the co-management of Whirinaki State Forest
with the East Coast Bay of Plenty Conservation Board, and that they get 640 hectares at
the 10 percent forestry allocation is certainly great. But I do want to mention Bill Bird
as one of the present leaders, even though he has passed on, because he was tenacious,
he was courageous, and he stood against all sorts of things, but sadly cancer took him
16 Feb 2012 Second Readings 561
away, and he never saw it. At times we me ntion people who are not here, but Bill was a
real warrior and I want to recognise that.
Ngāti Manawa, tēnā koutou. E mihi atu i a koutou e tū atu mō te take nei.
[Greetings Ngāti Manawa. I commend your stance on this matter.]
This deed was signed in December 2009, and th e iwi were part of the central North
Island forestry settlement negotiated by us  a long period of tim e ago. I do want to
recognise Ng āti Manawa’s efforts, the place that th ey have taken in these claims, and
how they have come forward on it.
For Ng āti P āhauwera, Tom Gemmell was like Bill Bi rd, a real warrior. And Toro
Waaka, Raymond, Joe, Megan, as the Minister of M āori Affairs mentioned, Charlie
Hirini, and all those ones who are not here, including Auntie Sophie Keefe—all of those
great people took this down the roadway. It is a great day, and Ng āti P āhauwera are
certainly working hard. They live on the banks of that great awa, M ōhaka. And then we
talk about water; it continually flows ther e and they have a hi gh opinion on who owns
it, what it is, and where it should be going. So I wish them all the best. In the sense of
the redress, it is important and significant to them.
In relation to the Ngati Porou Claims Settle ment Bill, one thing you learn is being a
Hauiti person you are Ngati Porou, and being Ngati Porou you are generally Hauiti.
Those things that create tensions are ther e, but certainly we look forward to supporting
the Minister to ensure that this has a speedy passageway to finality, and that we can all
celebrate with these iwi that have turned up here tonight. Tēnā koe.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations): These are four very important bills. Dr Sharples has outlined the essence
of the bills, but because of what I thought was an excellent contribution by Mr Jones,
and again by Mr Horomia, I just want to say that each of the settlements we are talking
about tonight raises an  important issue concerning water. There are four rivers that are
very much part and parcel  of the settlements, the M ōhaka, the Rangitaiki, the Waiap ū,
and the Waipā, and they are all slightly different versions of a genuine and sincere effort
by the Crown to involve iwi in the co-govern ance of those particular resources. They
are different models, but I believe they ar e going to be successful, and that they are
adapted to the particular needs of the iwi and the particular needs of the rivers
concerned—more about that in the course of the Committee stage.
The M āori Affairs Committee has considered these bills, it has submitted its
commentary on them to the House, and I want to thank Mr Henare and his team for the
very thorough examination of the bills. I want  to thank other Ministers and departments
involved in the process. A wi de variety of people from ac ross the politi cal spectrum
have made some very, very important contributions to these settlements over the years. I
particularly want to acknowledge Mr Ho romia and Mr Jones, who always put
partisanship to one side, and work with this Government on these issues, which is the
way it should be.
I also, briefly, just to show how bipartisan  I am, want to refer to the negotiators I
have been working with: Paul Swain for th e Crown with Ngati Porou, and Fran Wilde
for the Crown with Ng āti P āhauwera. What is it about fo rmer Labour MPs that they
make such very good Treaty negotiators? They are so pleasant to deal with when they
have left this place. Some, of course, I do not think could ever ch ange their spots, but
others are such very nice peopl e. In fact, it is an indica tion of how nice they are that—
again, to show how bipartisan I am; too bi partisan for my own good—I have asked Mr
Rick Barker, an excellent fellow, to work for me with Mr Swain in Taranaki.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Oh no. It is the qual ity of the contribution
they make. So there we have it. A lot of good work has been done on these bills. Let us
get down to the detail in the Committee stage.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: T ēnā koe. T ēnei e
tautoko ana ng ā mihi, ki ng ā iwi i tae mai nei ki te whakarongo ki a m ātau nei k ōrero.
Nō reira ki a koutou katoa, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou.
[Thank you. I endorse the acknowledgments to the tribes who have arrived here to
listen to our speeches. Hence, greetings to you all, greetings, greetings.]
This second reading opportunity is just  a brief chance for members of the M āori
Affairs Committee to report back on some ke y aspects of what they heard during the
select committee. Can I say first of all on  my part that although I am not a current
member of the M āori Affairs Committee, we were hosted with absolute hospitality and
respect. The role of the select committee I think is a difficult one, because there are
great expectations placed on what the sel ect committee should be doing at the point of
hearings when we go out into you r community. So can I say to Ng āti Manawa, Ng āti
Whare, Ng āti Pāhauwera, Ngati Porou, and Ng ā Wai o Maniapoto koutou katoa, for
your kind hospitality in hosting us the gratitude is ours.
Can I just point to some  comments for each of the settlements—firstly, Ng āti
Manawa and Ng āti Whare. Really, I think the things that stood out for me were issues
around representation on the Rangitaiki Rive r Forum. When we heard evidence from
Ngāti Haku Patuheuheu and about th eir claims to the Rangitaik i, and considered issues
around the Rangitaiki River Forum, we were  confident that th ere were enabling
provisions so that, at such a time when Ng āti Haku Patuheuheu wanted to be a part of
the forum, the model was there to enable that to happen.
Secondly, on the fisheries protocol as stated in the settlement, we were confident that
this was an opportunity for both Ng āti Manawa and Ng āti Whare to have a proactive
and ongoing role in the fisheries of their river, and we recommended no change. And,
thirdly, on the substantive issue of their maunga, T āwhiuau—and this is probably
something to highlight to the Minister fo r Treaty of Waitangi Ne gotiations—the select
committee members were quite mindful that if  another Treaty settlement impinged on
Ngāti Manawa’s interest in T āwhiuau, then this was a significant matter that the
Minister would have to pay attention to so that those rights were not infringed upon. I
wanted to highlight those issues in the sec ond reading, because they will be matters that
may need to be considered if  the Crown thinks it is going  to have other settlements
impinging upon its interest.
I want to go to Ng āti Pāhauwera briefly. Probably two issues stood out there. Firstly,
we did have representations to the select  committee that contested the mandate of
Pāhauwera. Having considered at length the aspects around the Pāhauwera mandate, the
select committee was confident—absolutely confident—in the mandate that was
expressed by P āhauwera and their ability to get to the point of settlement, and we did
not consider any substantive change to the legislation on this front.
This is an important questi on, I should mention, for all Treaty settlements, because
often claimants and cross-claimants come to the select committee table thinking that we
can change issues around this substantially. It is very difficult to do so. I want to
commend Te Ururoa Flavell, who chaired the committee for the hearing of this bill, and
I think he managed the process quite well, and to a positive outcome.
The definition of “Ng āti Pāhauwera”, and the interests of the Ng āi Tahu hap ū, was
one of those issues where we really found ourselves conflicted, and the same thing arose
in the Ngati Porou settlement. Members of the select committee did not think it was
beholden upon us to adjudicate over whakapapa within iwi. So on that basis, although
16 Feb 2012 Second Readings 563
we understand and heard the full representations of Ng āi Tahu hapū, we accept that for
the purposes of this settlement the definition of “Ngāti Pāhauwera” in the bill stands.
I want to move to a substantive lot of hearings that we had on the Ngati Porou
Claims Settlement Bill. I want to pay tribute to those who got this far, having heard the
number of cross-claimants who came to the hearings. You think you have got problems;
come to my place. We have got all sorts of things happening back home.
But can I say that one of the things that stood out in the Ngati Porou claim settlement
hearings at the select committee level was that there was this high sense of urgency
from many claimants that they did not ha ve the ability to have their historical
grievances aired. There is an innovation in th is particular settlement around an airing-
of-grievances process that I understand is being proposed.
Again, one of the issues that really st ood out substantially in this particular
settlement is that people need the opportunity to have their histories told and captured in
some shape and form, so that they are on the historical record. Again, we were not in a
position—and we do not feel as select committ ee members that we should have been in
the position—to adjudicate over whakapapa. That is solely for Ngati Porou to
determine. But the process, in  itself, if there is the oppor tunity through the airing-of-
grievances part of this particular settle ment that histories can be heard, told, and
captured, should be considered as a positive part of giving a complete picture.
I certainly want to pay tr ibute to Api Mahuika, who act ually personally bore the
brunt of a lot of criticisms at the select committee table. I can say from some personal
reflection that the position he holds is not an easy one. It is thankless, and you bear a lot
of responsibility with little gratitude afterwards. But can  I say that the dignity with
which the claim was put to the select committee had a strong bearing on my view that
this is the best opportunity for Ngati Por ou going forward and for the generations to
come. What stood out even more was that th ere was a firm focus on this being an
opportunity for the next generation to move forward.
Finally, I come back to my home town in a sense, and that is Ngā Wai o Maniapoto. I
want to, in this second reading, highlight tw o particular aspects—maybe three. First is
the interests of Raukawa in Wharep ūhunga. They came to the select committee with a
representation that the select committee should change or broaden the reach of Raukawa
in terms of the Wharep ūhunga. The select committee took  that on board but did not
think that any change to the legislation was necessary. However, I would urge the
Minister to seek some confirmation from the Office of Treaty Settlements that the
memorandum of understanding that has been reached between Raukawa and Maniapoto
will be confirmed before the third reading, because this will be a positive part of
ensuring that both Raukawa and Maniapoto interests in the Waipā will be clearly stated.
Second is the issue of the clean-up fund being added to the Waikato River Authority.
It is not the outcome that Maniapoto was seeking, but is an opportunity to have issues of
clean-up addressed. But the real issue ther e will be Waikato and Maniapoto assuring
themselves that the ongoing aspects of cl ean-up of the upper river catchment are a
matter yet to be negotiated with the Crown, and should be a matter supported by
Waikato in the overall interests of having a clean Waip ā, so that we get a clean Waikato
River. In terms of the Lower Waip ā catchment, I am confiden t that with a bit of
common sense and a bit of time both Waikato and Maniapoto will sort out its interests
and how to manage aspects in the Lower Waipā catchment.
Overall, this feels like a ru shed process, but it is only the sec ond readings. I am
confident that in the third reading of the legislation members will be able to focus on
those settlements that they want to highlight , in terms of the opportunities they provide
for the people going forward. Nō reira, ki a koutou katoa, tēnā tātou.
564 Second Readings 16 Feb 2012

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker Robertson. Kia ora an ō tātou katoa. Me whakar āpopoto i taku k ōrero i te mea
kua oti kē i a au te kōrero mō tētahi wāhanga. Ēngari, kua oti kē te wāhi ki te Minita. Ko
te wāhi ki a au ko te Pāti Māori me te kī atu, ka tautoko ake i tēnei o ngā pire kei pōhēhē
koutou, kāre te P āti Māori i te tautoko i te karanga. Ā, ēngari paku k ōrero. Tuatahi hai
whaiwhai haere i te āhuatanga o te kōrero a te Hōnore Parekura Horomia, e tangi ana te
ngākau mō te Bill Bird rā, tērā o ngā tāngata i kaha ki te kawe i tēnei o ngā take ki mua i
te aroaro o ng ā momo Minita. K āo. Ki mua i te aroaro o ng ā Minita i ng ā tau kua hipa
ake. E tangi ana te ngākau ki a ia, otirā, ki a rātau. Tērā Māori, kātahi te tangata māia ko
tērā.
Me wero tonu i te H ōnore Shane Jones. E k ī, e k ī? He w āhi obscure a Minginui, he
wāhi obscure a Murupara. Come on. Ng āti Manawa, Ng āti Whare m āku tēnā kōrero i
whakatika.
E tika ana te k ōrero a w ētahi atu p ērā i a Nanaia Mahuta, ē, ko ētahi o ng ā iwi ka
titiro mai ki te K āwanatanga, ki te komiti wh āiti, te select committee, ki te k ī mai m ā
koutou, m ā te K āwanatanga, m ā te Karauna r ānei e whakatikatika ng ā kōrero ā-
whakapapa. Ko tāku ko te k ī atu e k āo, mā ngā iwi tērā e whakatika, kaua m ā te Whare
Pāremata. Ko ētahi ka kī, ka noho me k ī, tata nei, whanaunga nei ēngari, kei te kī atu ki
te Kāwanatanga, nō mātau tēnei whenua, me k ōrero ki a m ātau mō te whakahoki mai i
wā mātau whenua. E k āo, m ā ng ā iwi an ō rā tērā take e k ōrero. N ō reira, he nui ng ā
kōrero i puta hei whaiwhai haere i tana kōrero.
Nō mātau te waimarie kia tae atu ki a koutou Ng āti Pāhauwera ki tā koutou marae ka
mutu, ki Tikitiki. Ahakoa i wepua au e w ētahi ēngari, he pai tonu te  noho ki waenganui
i ērā momo take, he akoranga nui ki a au, ā-tiamana nei. Engari, n ōku te waimarie kia
tae atu ki reira ki waenganui i a koutou. I te pērā anō ki a koutou o Ngāti Maniapoto, i tā
mātau taenga atu ki tērā o ngā whare, te Tokanganui-a-Noho. Ka mutu, i roto i te rohe o
Te Waiariki, ko Ngāti Whare me Ngāti Manawa, e noho tata nei nā runga i te āhuatanga
o te ara whanaunga, ar ā, ko Te Wharep ākau rāua Tangiharuru. Ko koutou an ō koutou.
Nō reira, ko tāku noa ake he k ī atu, ka pai, ka pai. Aki ākina, akiākina ngā pire nei kia
eke ki te taumata e tika ana.
Nō reira kāti, koinei te kōrero a te Pāti Māori, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou. Kua tata eke,
kua tata eke. Kia hoki mai ki te w āhanga whakamutunga, ka āhua whakatōroangia pea
ngā kōrero mā te rua tekau meneti. Hoi anō, tērā kōrero tērā. Kia ora tātau.
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Roberts on, and greetings once aga in to us all. I
will shorten my address, as I have already spoken at length about a part of the
legislation. The part relating to the Minister has been covered already, so my part is to
talk about the Māori Party, and say that we endorse this legislation, in case you wonder
whether the M āori Party supports it, although the call is a short one. In the first
instance, and to follow up the tenor of the sentiments expressed by the Hon Parekura
Horomia, the heart mourns the passing of Bill Bird, a man who worked hard to bring
this legislation before the va rious kinds of Minist ers; not true—Ministers in past years.
The heart weeps for him, and indeed for them. That M āori, what a courageous one he
was.
I continue to challenge the Hon Shane J ones when he asserts that Minginui and
Murupara are obscure places. Come on! How true is that? Get it right. Ng āti Manawa
and Ngāti Whare, I will correct that assertion.
Some of the statements by ot her speakers are absolutely correct, such as those of the
Hon Nanaia Mahuta. Some tribes are lookin g at the Government, at the select
committee process, and saying: leave it up to  the Government or the Crown to rectify
any issues about genealogy. I say no—tribes are responsible for that, and not the House
of Parliament. Some very close relatives ar e saying to the Government: this land is
16 Feb 2012 Second Readings 565
ours, talk to us about giving it back. Not so, that sort of issue is for the tribes to deal to.
So a lot of talk has emerged to follow up her assertion.
It was our good fortune getting to you, Ng āti Pāhauwera, to your marae, and then
moving on to Tikitiki. Even though I might hav e taken a bit of a whipping from some
there, it was still good to be amongst you in those kinds of issues, and a huge learning
curve for me as chairman. But I still considered myself lucky to be there amongst you. It
was like that with you, Ng āti Maniapoto, when we arrived at Tokanganui-a-Noho, that
ancestral house of all ancestral houses. So to the region of Te Waiariki, to Ng āti Whare
and Ngāti Manawa, who are closely related through Te Wharep ākau and Tangiharuru.
You are really one and the same. So I simply want to say: well done, great. Move and
urge these bills along to a level most fitting for them.
Enough for now. Congratulations  and well done from the M āori Party. It is almost
there, nearly. When we come back for the final part we may extend our address by 20
minutes. Who knows what will happen. Congratulations to us all.]

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I would like to acknowle dge Ngati Porou in the
House. After all, Sir Apirana Ngata would, I imagine, be very, very proud. With each
settlement we come together and we cast away that which has divided us, and in
settlement we embrace that which unites us—our land, our water, our people, our
wairua. With each settlement we grow togeth er as a country, as a nation, and as New
Zealanders we all have a vested interest in the success of these bills.
Now, as Ngāti Maniapoto, I must also declare an in terest. I am one of that sprawling
brood of Ormsbys, and I am burstin g with joy that the sacred water of my iwi is to be
protected and nurtured, to be cleaned, to honour the wairua. Recognising and addressing
the grievances of all before us tonight is paramount. It has taken New Zealand many
years to reach this point. Again, I acknow ledge all of you—all of us—who are here
today, because we represent so much more. Together, we represent the many who have
gone before us, the many who cannot be here  today. I look forwar d to working at the
Committee stage to ensure that the full intent of these settlements is achieved. As it has
taken so long to get to this point, and as th ere is yet a small way to  go, I do not wish to
take more of this time, but I endorse on be half of New Zealand First the progress of
these bills in this Whare. Thank you.
